Hey, Dear Future Company Secretary.

4 min read

Yes, YOU.
It's just a matter of time.
(Your future self, whispering.)

There are probably a hundred questions running through your mind right now. Should I really pursue CS? Can I clear it? How difficult is it? Which teacher should I choose? What should I study? What if I fail? What happens after CS? Will this qualification actually change my life? I know these questions because I was once the student asking them too.

I started this journey without having all the answers. In the first year of my graduation, I gave the CSEET examination almost out of curiosity. I kept going, pursued my MBA alongside CS, completed my training and eventually cleared all the CS examinations before completing my post-graduation. Am I telling you this to flex? Maybe a little. And honestly, I don't think there is anything wrong with that.

Sometimes, you need a little ego. Not the kind that makes you believe you are better than everyone else, but the kind that makes you say, “Let's see what I am capable of.” The kind that makes you sit down and study when you don't feel like it. The kind that makes you want to prove something to yourself. There will be days when motivation disappears, when the syllabus feels endless and when you start questioning whether you can actually finish what you started. On those days, maybe you need something as simple as your own ego telling you, “You started this. Now let's see if you can finish it.”

Do it for the ego. Do it because you want to know what you are capable of. Do it because there is a version of you somewhere in the future who knows that you could have done more. Do it because one day you may want to look back at the person you were when you started and say, “I told you we'd make it.”

But I am not writing this book simply to tell you about my journey. I am writing it because I remember what it felt like to have questions and not have anyone around me who could give me a straight answer. You search online, ask seniors, watch videos, read opinions and somehow end up even more confused because everyone seems to have a different answer. So you start figuring things out yourself, one mistake and one experience at a time.

Somewhere between that student and the person I am today, I had a thought: What if I could go back and talk to my previous self? What if I could sit beside that version of me and answer the questions he desperately wanted someone to answer? What would I tell him before he started? Which mistakes would I tell him to avoid? What would I tell him about studying, teachers, training, failure, money, career, communication and everything else that nobody really explains when you begin?

I cannot actually go back and have that conversation. But I can write this book.

So that's what I am doing.

This is not a perfect roadmap, and it is certainly not a guarantee of success. I am not going to tell you that if you follow everything in this book, your career will magically work out. This is simply my attempt to share what I learned while figuring things out for myself. Some of it may work for you, some of it may not, and that's completely fine. Take what is useful, question what isn't and build your own way.

This book is for the student who has just started, the student who is confused, the student who is questioning whether they are capable of doing this and the student who has a hundred questions but nobody to ask. I was that student once. I know what it feels like to stand at the beginning of something without knowing exactly where it will take you.

And now, I am writing to you from a little further down the road.

If something I learned can save you from a mistake, answer a question, give you a different perspective or simply make you feel a little less alone in this journey, then this book has done its job.

You don't need to have everything figured out today. You don't even need to be the smartest person in the room. You just need to start, keep learning and keep showing up. And somewhere along the way, you may discover that you are capable of much more than you originally thought.

So, Future Company Secretary, take the course seriously, but don't take yourself too seriously. Work hard, question things, make mistakes, learn from them and, when necessary, let your ego push you a little further.

Do it for EGO.

Why Burn the Sea?

2 min read

You might be wondering why I called this book Burn the Sea. It sounds a little crazy, and honestly, that is the point. The idea came from something I started believing during my own CS journey: sometimes you need enough ego to attempt what looks impossible.

For me, the CS course felt like a sea. Not because clearing CS is some impossible, world-changing achievement. It isn't. There are much harder things in life. But if you have compared CS with an ordinary graduation examination, you already know that it demands a different level of consistency. There is a huge syllabus, multiple subjects, amendments, revisions, examinations, failures and months of preparation. You cannot simply wake up a few days before the exam, read the important chapters and expect everything to work out. It takes time, patience and, frankly, guts.

That is why I imagine the CS course as a sea. When you stand at the shore, it looks enormous. You cannot see the other side. You don't know exactly how long it will take, how many times you will have to swim back, or how tired you will become along the way. You can spend months staring at the sea, researching the perfect way to cross it, asking other people whether it is possible and worrying about how difficult it will be. Or you can get into the water and start swimming.

But I wanted something more than simply crossing the sea.

I wanted to burn it.

Not literally, of course. The idea is absurd, and that is exactly why I like it. When something feels overwhelmingly large, sometimes the only way to approach it is with an unreasonable amount of belief in yourself. You study like a maniac, you keep showing up, you solve another question, revise another chapter, sit for another test and keep going even when the course seems endless. Your ego keeps telling you, “You started this. Now finish it.”

Eventually, the sea that once looked impossible starts disappearing behind you.

That is what Burn the Sea means to me. It is not about pretending that CS is impossible. It is about developing the courage to take on something difficult with enough determination that, by the time you are finished, you can look back and wonder why you were ever so afraid of it.

And this idea goes beyond CS. There will be many things in your life that look too large when you first see them. A difficult career, a business you want to build, a skill you want to master, a financial goal, a personal challenge or simply a version of yourself that seems far away. You may not always know exactly how you are going to get there.

You don't need to.

Sometimes you just need enough fire to take the first step. So, if CS is the sea, let your ego be the fire.

Study hard. Study relentlessly. Take the course seriously. Give yourself permission to believe that you can do something difficult before you have any evidence that you can. And when the course feels too big, don't stand at the shore calculating how deep the water is.

Get in.
Swim.
And if you have to—

Burn the Sea.

Why CS

2 min read

Why should you choose this career when there are so many options?

Let me be brutally honest: CS is not the best career for everyone, and it is certainly not a guaranteed path to a high-paying job. If you are choosing it simply because someone told you, “Beta, CS kar lo, future secure hai,” stop and think. You are potentially committing three to five years of your life to this course, so you should know what you are getting into.

What makes CS attractive, at least to me, is its potential return on your time, effort and money. You can enter your professional life with a recognised qualification, specialised knowledge and exposure to how companies, Boards, laws, regulations and business decisions actually work. Over time, that foundation can take you in many directions—compliance, governance, law, finance, management, consulting, practice, or even something of your own. Your qualification does not decide where you eventually end up; it gives you a platform to build from.

I also believe CS is particularly interesting for someone who does not have the luxury of spending years experimenting with different careers. The financial investment is relatively manageable compared with many professional or postgraduate routes, but the real price is your time and energy. You may spend years studying after college or alongside work, and the examinations will demand much more than simply memorising a syllabus. You will have to learn how to sit with difficult subjects, deal with failure, work without motivation and keep going when the result is uncertain.

So, what does it take? Time, serious effort and a relatively modest financial investment. The exact cost will depend on how you prepare, but the bigger investment is the years you put into becoming qualified.

And that is why I would not sell CS to you as an “easy” or “secure” career. It isn't. But if you are willing to make that trade, the course can give you something valuable: a professional foundation that can compound for decades. Even if you eventually move beyond traditional CS work, the understanding of business, law, governance and responsibility can stay with you.

Clearing CS is not a small achievement. It requires you to do something difficult repeatedly, even when you don't feel like doing it. And perhaps that is one of the most valuable things the course can teach you: not merely how to become a Company Secretary, but how to take on something difficult and see it through.

That is the trade. A few years of your life, a lot of effort, and a relatively small financial investment in exchange for a qualification that can become the foundation of your professional life.

Whether that trade is worth it for you is something only you can decide.

1

How to Approach This Course?

3 min read

Your approach should be simple: get the course completed. CS/CA/CMA are professional courses, and you will get the maximum output by getting them done in the least time possible. Ideally, if you clear all the exams in the first attempt and do your internship simultaneously, you can finish the course in around three years. But if you have multiple attempts or start your internship only after clearing all your exams, the journey can easily extend by another year. This path will be full of hustle, but it will make you stronger for sure. You may go through a phase where you wake up tired, get ready for your internship, rush to the office, spend 8–10 hours at work, come home and study for another four hours, and then go to bed late only to wake up tired again. Haa haa. (I chose this path, where I was doing an MBA + CS Professional studies + CS internship.)

But don't worry if you cannot commit to this. You have other options and other paths as well. We have enough examples of people who chose different routes and still reached the same destination: becoming a CS. It is completely fine if you choose one group at a time and clear it in one go. Taking up an internship alongside your studies can save time and help you start earning earlier, while taking both groups together and starting an internship later for a higher stipend is also a valid choice. There is no single correct path. It depends on your priorities—time, money or effort. The only thing that ultimately matters is that you clear the exam. That's it.

Go on YouTube and search “CS journey” or “CS preparation journey”. You will find plenty of people who chose different paths, took different numbers of attempts, started training at different stages and still reached the same destination. Watch a few of them, understand the options available to you and then choose your own way. Don't copy someone else's journey blindly. Take the information, understand your priorities and make your own decision.

I can't tell you to do this or do that, or tell you to follow this path instead of that one. From the outside, it may look like everyone is pursuing the same course, writing the same examinations and working towards the same qualification. But in reality, everyone is living a completely different story. Everyone has different circumstances, different responsibilities, different resources, different fears and different priorities. At some point, everyone has to make difficult choices, and there is no universal formula for making them. What worked for one person may not work for you, and that is completely fine.

Everybody is the hero of their own story. You are the hero of yours. Think of yourself as the main character. Not in the sense that the world revolves around you, but in the sense that you are responsible for deciding how you respond to what happens to you. You will fail, make wrong decisions, change your mind, start again, lose confidence and sometimes wonder whether you are even on the right path. That is part of the story.

Be the main character of your story.

Approach this journey in the way that makes sense for you. Choose the path you would be proud to narrate years from now. Maybe your story will be about clearing everything in the first attempt. Maybe it will involve failures, changing strategies, working alongside your studies, taking longer than expected or taking a completely different route. You don't need someone else's story to validate yours.

Think about the person you want to become when you look back at these years. What choices would that person be proud of? What risks would they wish you had taken? What would they regret not trying? You don't have to make every decision perfectly. You just have to make your decisions consciously and be willing to own the consequences.

So don't just complete the course. Live your version of the journey. Make the choices. Own the mistakes. Learn from them. And make sure that when you look back, you can say: this was my story, and I chose how to write it.

2

Solve the Right Problem

2 min read

As a professional-course student, you need to be very clear about what is most important to you right now. Then give it your maximum time, attention and energy.

I know you may have a lot of problems—family problems, financial problems, relationship problems, career problems, personal problems, this problem and that problem. But there is one thing you need to understand: you have limited attention. And if you genuinely want to clear your professional exams, you cannot give 50% of your attention to studying and the other 50% to everything going wrong in your life. You have to prioritise. Ask yourself: “Which problem can I actually solve right now? Why is it important right now, and how am I going to solve it?”

If your financial situation is so serious that you need to address it first, then do that. Take a step back from studying, solve what you can, create some stability, and then return to your preparation. But if a problem is completely beyond your control right now, worrying about it for hours will not solve it. Do what is in your control.

There is a beautiful line by Viktor Frankl: “When we are no longer able to change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.” I also believe this applies to anxiety. Sometimes anxiety grows because we know there is something we can do, but we are not doing it. You cannot control your family situation. You cannot control someone else's behaviour. You cannot control what happened yesterday. But you can control whether you study today. And sometimes, the best way to deal with a problem indirectly is to become stronger, more capable and more independent.

“The magic you are looking for is in the work you are avoiding.” So study. Study with all your heart. Study consistently, even when you don't feel motivated. Because sometimes, the thing you are avoiding is actually the thing that can change your life.

I learned this myself. When I was preparing for my CS Executive examinations, there were several problems at home. I spent a lot of time trying to manage everything simultaneously. I was silently carrying the stress and losing days to anxiety. Eventually, I realised something: I couldn't solve everything at that moment, but I could study.

So I stopped trying to control everything and started focusing on the one thing that was in my control. I cleared my CS Executive Group 1.

3

Sacrifice Is Overrated

3 min read

“The difference between successful people and really successful people is that really successful people say no to almost everything.” — Warren Buffett

You have to sacrifice everything! Yes, you hear this all the time. “You have to make sacrifices to become a CA/CS/CMA.” Bullshit. Really, tell me honestly—which profession, meaningful work or worthwhile goal does not demand something from you? Everything worth building has an opportunity cost. Stop romanticising it. You don't need to suffer, destroy your social life or make yourself miserable just to prove that you are serious about your career. You simply need to understand what matters to you and be willing to choose it over things that matter less, at least for a certain period.

(I am editing this book after spending more than eight hours at the office. It is AGM time, 11 September 2026, and I am sick too. ) So what?

Honestly, it doesn't feel like I am making some heroic sacrifice by sitting here and working on the book. I chose this. I wanted to write it. I wanted to finish it. I knew it would require time, energy and some uncomfortable days, and I was willing to give them. Do it, man. You chose this. You want to clear the exam. You know it requires consistent effort, discipline and a certain amount of your time. So give it. Stop complaining about the price after you have already decided that you want the result.

If you set a weekly target and fail to achieve it, then maybe this weekend you have to say no to a family function. Maybe you say no to your friends. Maybe you skip the movie, the trip, the party or the pointless two-hour scrolling session. So what? You are not sacrificing your entire life. You are choosing one thing over another. You cannot give equal time and attention to everything and then expect one thing to become exceptional. If clearing your exam is the priority for these few months, then studying gets priority. Not because your friends are bad, not because your family doesn't matter and certainly not because suffering makes you successful. It gets priority because you decided that this matters more right now.

That is what discipline actually is. It is not telling everyone, “Look how much I am sacrificing.” It is quietly saying, “I know what I want, so I know what I need to say no to.” And sometimes that no will disappoint people. You will miss a celebration. Your friends will go somewhere without you. Your family may not understand why you cannot attend something. You may sit at home while everyone else is having fun. That's okay. You are not saying no forever. You are saying not right now. There is a season for everything—a season to study, a season to work, a season to build and a season to celebrate. The mistake is expecting yourself to live every season at the same time.

And here is the part you need to accept: nobody is coming to protect your priorities for you. Your friends won't cancel the party because you have an exam. Your phone won't stop distracting you. Instagram won't tell you to close the app and study. Your problems won't politely wait until your attempt is over. You have to make that decision yourself. If you keep saying yes to everything, don't complain later that you didn't have enough time for the thing you claimed was most important.

So stop asking, “What am I sacrificing?” Ask, “What am I choosing?” That question changes everything. When you genuinely choose something, what you give up for it doesn't always feel like a sacrifice. It feels like a decision. And you don't need to explain every decision to everyone. No is a complete sentence. You don't need permission to protect your time, your attention or your future.

You are not required to sacrifice everything. You are required to choose deliberately. If you want the qualification, prepare for it. If you want the career, build for it. If you want the result, pay the price it actually requires. Not more. Not less. And when the time comes to look back, I hope you don't remember these months as the time you “sacrificed your life.” I hope you remember them as the time you decided what your life was worth building.

4

What Can You Expect From This Career?

15 min read

If you have just started the Company Secretary course, you probably have a lot of questions. You may not ask them openly, but they are somewhere in your mind. Will becoming a CS actually change my life? Will I get a good job? How much money can I expect? Will I have a secure career? Will people respect me? What if I am not among the smartest students in my batch? What if I clear the course but still don't know what I want to do? And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all—was choosing CS actually the right decision?

I don't want to answer these questions by giving you the usual motivational speech. You will hear enough of that during your journey. You will be told that CS is a prestigious profession, that there are countless opportunities, that companies always need CS professionals and that if you work hard, everything will eventually work out. Some of that is true. But it is not the whole truth. Every career has opportunities, competition, uncertainty, boring days, failures, lucky breaks and difficult decisions. CS is no different. So, before you spend the next few years preparing for this qualification, I think you deserve to know what you can realistically expect from this career. And I want to make one thing clear from the beginning: this chapter is not written to convince you that CS is the best career. If you have already chosen CS, my job is not to sell it to you. My job is to help you understand the road you have chosen. Because there is a big difference between completing a professional course and actually building a professional career. Clearing the examination is an achievement. What you do after clearing it is your career.

Will becoming a CS actually change your life?

Yes, but probably not in the way you are imagining right now. A professional qualification can change the opportunities available to you. It can give you access to jobs, responsibilities, people and conversations that may not have been available to you before. It can give you a professional identity and a foundation on which you can build for decades. But the certificate itself does not suddenly transform your personality, your income, your confidence or your life. You can become a CS and still be confused about your career. You can qualify and get a job that you don't enjoy. You can earn a decent salary and still feel financially insecure. You can work in a prestigious company and still feel that you are not growing. And you can start your career at a salary that feels disappointing today and, ten years later, build a career that you could not have imagined when you were a student. This is something I wish more students understood early. A qualification changes your starting position; it does not decide your final destination.

Think of CS as giving you a better set of cards to play with. It does not guarantee that you will win the game. You still have to learn how to play, understand the people around you, recognise opportunities, make good decisions and sometimes take risks. Two people can start with exactly the same qualification and have completely different careers. One may remain stuck for years doing repetitive work, while another may eventually become a senior professional, advisor, business owner or a trusted person in important corporate decisions. The difference is rarely the letters “CS” written after their names. The difference is what they built on top of those letters.

Will I earn good money after CS?

This is probably the most common question, and there is nothing wrong with asking it. Money matters. You need money to live, support your family, build security, travel, invest and enjoy your life. We should not pretend that money is unimportant just because we are talking about a professional course.

But here is the honest answer: CS can give you a good income, but it does not guarantee a high income.

Your first salary may actually disappoint you. You may spend several years studying, sacrificing weekends, clearing difficult examinations and finally qualify, only to receive an offer that makes you wonder whether all those years were worth it. Don't panic. Your first salary is not a valuation of your potential. It is simply the price the market is willing to pay for your current level of experience. The uncomfortable truth is that the market does not pay you merely because you worked hard to pass an examination. It pays you for the problems you can solve.

A newly qualified CS who knows the syllabus may still have limited practical value. A CS with three or four years of experience who can independently handle important compliance, understand regulatory consequences, communicate with senior management and take responsibility for difficult situations can be worth considerably more. Later, a professional who understands not only compliance but also business, finance, securities law, transactions and governance can become even more valuable.

So don't ask only, “What is the salary of a CS?” Ask, “What kind of CS professional am I becoming?”

There is a huge difference between being qualified and being valuable.

If I work hard, will I definitely succeed?

No.

I know that is not the answer students usually want to hear, but it is the answer I think they need to hear. Hard work is necessary, but hard work alone is not a guarantee of success. You can work extremely hard in the wrong direction. You can spend ten years doing the same work without actually becoming better at it. You can collect certificates without developing useful skills. You can study for long hours without understanding what you are studying. You can even be the most hardworking person in the room and still lose an opportunity to someone who understands the situation better. That does not mean hard work is useless. It means hard work needs direction.

Your career will be influenced by your knowledge, your decisions, your communication, your ability to learn, the people you work with, the opportunities you receive and, yes, sometimes luck. You cannot control all of these things. But you can increase the probability of a good outcome.

Study seriously. Work seriously. Learn from good people. Take responsibility. Develop skills. Build relationships. Keep yourself relevant. When an opportunity appears, be prepared enough to take it. You cannot control everything about your career. But you can control whether you are ready when the opportunity arrives.

Will people respect me after I become a CS?

This is another question that students rarely ask directly. There is a strange thing about professional qualifications: the respect you imagine before qualifying and the respect you experience after qualifying are often very different.

When you are studying, you may imagine that once you become a CS, everyone will know what you do and automatically respect you. That is not how it works.

There will be people who don't know what a Company Secretary does. Some will confuse it with CA. Some will ask why you didn't become a lawyer. Some may not even understand why companies need a CS. Don't take it personally. Most people simply have no reason to know the profession in detail.

But professional reputation works differently.

A CFO who trusts your judgement matters more than ten strangers who know your designation. A CEO who calls you before making an important decision matters more than someone congratulating you on LinkedIn. A senior professional who recommends you for an opportunity because they know your work matters more than having thousands of social-media followers.

That is the kind of reputation you should build. Don't work to become famous. Work to become trusted. Fame can come and go very quickly. Trust takes years to build and can stay with you for decades.

Will CS give me job security?

Here I want to make an important distinction. No career can give you absolute job security. A company can restructure. A business can shut down. Management can change. Technology can replace certain tasks. A better candidate can come along. Economic conditions can change. Your job can disappear even if you have done nothing wrong. But some professions have stronger structural demand than others because the work they perform is connected to continuing legal or regulatory requirements. CS is one of them.

Companies continue to have legal and governance obligations. Boards continue to meet. Shareholders continue to have rights. Listed companies continue to have disclosure requirements. Regulatory frameworks continue to evolve. Businesses continue to undertake transactions that require legal and compliance judgement. That creates a strong underlying need for professionals who understand these systems.

But don't make the mistake of thinking that this automatically makes you secure.

If your entire value is that you know how to prepare a particular form, someone may eventually automate it, outsource it or teach another person to do it. If your value is that you can understand a complicated situation, identify the risk, explain it clearly to management and help the company find a practical way forward, you become much harder to replace.

This is why I prefer the term career security over job security. Don't spend your career trying to make sure nobody can fire you. Spend your career becoming someone who can always find a way to create value somewhere.

Do I have to be brilliant to succeed?

Probably not.

You don't have to be the smartest student in your batch to build a good career. In fact, professional life often rewards qualities that examinations cannot properly measure.

Can people trust you?

Can you communicate clearly?

Can you admit when you don't know something?

Can you learn quickly?

Can you take responsibility when something goes wrong?

Can you remain calm when everyone else is panicking?

Can you understand what your senior actually needs instead of simply doing exactly what you were told?

Can you work with difficult people without becoming difficult yourself? These things matter.

At the beginning of your career, intelligence may get you noticed. But reliability gets you responsibility. Over time, judgement gets you influence.

And judgement is something you develop by doing real work, making mistakes, observing experienced professionals and thinking deeply about why things happen.

So don't waste your student years worrying about whether someone else is smarter than you.

Become more capable than you were six months ago. That is a much better competition.

What if I don't know what I want to become?

Then you are completely normal.

When you are eighteen, twenty or twenty-two, society somehow expects you to decide what you want to do for the next forty years of your life. I don't think that is realistic. You may start your CS journey thinking you want to work in a big listed company and later discover that you love practice. You may think you want corporate law and discover that you enjoy governance. You may enter compliance and eventually move towards management. You may even discover that traditional CS work is not what you want at all.

That does not mean you failed.

Your first job is not a lifetime contract. Your first salary is not your final salary.

Your first designation is not your identity.

Your twenties should partly be about collecting evidence about yourself. Try things. Work with different people. Observe what kind of work gives you energy and what kind drains you. Pay attention to what you naturally become good at.

You don't need to know the final destination on day one. You just need to make sure that the direction you are moving in is making you better.

Then what will actually make me different from thousands of other CS professionals?

This is perhaps the most important question of the entire chapter. Because there will be thousands of people who have the same qualification as you.

Your certificate will say Company Secretary. So will theirs.

Your marks may be different. Your college may be different. Your first company may be different. But eventually the market starts asking a different question:

“What are you particularly good at?”

Being a CS professional is your professional identity. It is not necessarily your differentiation.

Maybe you become extremely good at handling listed-company compliance. Maybe you understand securities law better than most people around you. Maybe you become excellent at Board communication. Maybe you understand corporate transactions. Maybe you become a brilliant secretarial auditor. Maybe you become the person everyone calls when a difficult governance problem appears. You don't have to become the best at everything. Become unusually good at something useful.

That is how you start creating a professional moat. And this doesn't mean that you should start collecting twenty certificates immediately. It means that as you gain experience, you should notice where your natural interest and market demand overlap. That intersection can become your strength.

Should I only focus on my studies right now?

If you are preparing for an examination, yes, you should take your studies seriously. But don't make the mistake of believing that passing examinations is the same thing as preparing for your career.

Your books will teach you what companies are supposed to do. Your training will begin showing you what companies actually do. Your career will teach you why they do it.

There is a difference.

While studying, learn to communicate. Learn to write properly. Understand basic finance and accounting. Read annual reports. Follow what is happening in the business world. Learn how technology is changing professional work. Observe how experienced people communicate with each other. Learn how to ask questions.

One day, nobody will ask you how many hours you studied for your examination. They will give you a problem and ask, “Can you handle this?”

That is when the transition from student to professional really begins.

How should I think about building my career?

I think you should start thinking about this question earlier than most people do.

Do you want money? Of course. But perhaps you also want freedom, meaningful work, learning, good relationships, health, peace of mind or the ability to control your own time.

These things may sound unrelated to a professional course, but they are not. Your career will occupy a significant part of your life. So you should think not only about what job you want, but also about what kind of life you want your work to help you build.

This is one of the biggest shifts in perspective I personally got from reading The Almanack of Naval Ravikant, compiled by Eric Jorgenson.

A book that changed how I think about career and money

If you have never heard of Naval Ravikant, he is an entrepreneur, investor and thinker whose ideas cover wealth, work, judgement, leverage and happiness. I am not recommending the book because I want you to become obsessed with making money. In fact, it had almost the opposite effect on me.

What affected me most was the way his ideas made me question what I actually expect from my career and, eventually, from my life.

We spend years preparing for a profession. We worry about salary, designation, company, promotion and status. But very rarely do we stop and ask: What do I actually want my career to help me build?

For me, this is probably the one book that has changed my perspective on money and happiness the most. I have recommended it and gifted it to almost everyone I have met whom I felt could benefit from it. The book is also freely available online, https://navalmanack.s3.amazonaws.com/Eric- Jorgenson_The-Almanack-of-Naval-Ravikant_Final.pdf so you don't necessarily need to buy it to read it. (search: almanac of Naval Ravikant book pdf)

You may disagree with Naval on many things. That's perfectly fine. You don't have to accept someone's philosophy completely for it to make you think differently.

I would simply recommend reading it once.

Not because you need to start thinking about becoming rich when you have just started CS, but because you should start thinking early about what you actually want your work to do for your life.

So, what should you actually do from here?

First, clear the course. It sounds obvious, but sometimes students become so obsessed with planning their future that they forget to finish what is immediately in front of them. Your first responsibility is to build the foundation.

Second, get real exposure. Don't be afraid of ordinary work during your training. Preparing documents, checking compliances, making notes, attending meetings and doing repetitive tasks may not feel exciting. But if you pay attention, these things teach you how organisations actually function. Don't just complete the task; understand why the task exists.

Third, develop skills that your syllabus cannot completely teach you. Learn to communicate. Learn to write. Understand business. Understand basic finance. Learn technology. Learn how to use AI responsibly. Learn how to present an idea. These skills may not directly appear in your examination, but they will appear repeatedly throughout your career.

Fourth, build your reputation before you think you need one. You don't need to become an influencer. You don't need thousands of followers. Just become known among the people you work with as someone who is sincere, reliable, curious and capable. Your reputation will often travel further than your resume. (detailed version in upcoming chapters)

And finally, don't rush.

You will see someone qualify before you. Someone will get a better package. Someone will join a bigger company. Someone will have a better LinkedIn profile. Someone will appear to be moving much faster than you.

Let them.

You are not running their race.

Your career is not a two-year competition. It is potentially a forty-year journey.

At twenty-two, a difference of ₹10,000 in your monthly salary may feel enormous. Ten years later, the person who kept learning, built strong relationships, developed judgement and became genuinely valuable may be in a completely different position.

So don't obsess over where you are today. Ask yourself a better question:

“Am I becoming more valuable every year?” If the answer continues to be yes, you are probably moving in the right direction.

The truth about choosing CS

If you came into CS expecting the qualification to automatically give you money, respect and security, I would lower those expectations.

If you came into CS expecting nothing but struggle, I would also change that expectation.

The truth lies somewhere in between.

CS can give you a strong professional foundation. It can expose you to companies, Boards, laws, regulations, business decisions and senior professionals. It can provide a specialised career with several directions in which you can grow. It can give you a stable profession and, for those who become genuinely good at what they do, significant financial and professional upside.

But none of that happens automatically.

The qualification opens the door.

You still have to walk through it. You still have to learn, fail, find your strengths, build relationships, earn trust and make yourself valuable and eventually, you have to decide what kind of professional—and what kind of person—you want to become. So, if you have just started your CS journey, don't worry about having everything figured out. You don't need to. Take the course seriously. Learn beyond the course. Get your hands dirty with real work. Stay curious. Develop your communication. Understand people. Understand business. Use technology instead of fearing it. Build a good reputation. And keep asking yourself whether the person you are becoming is someone you would be proud to work with.

5

How to Research Well

Teachers, Classes, Books, Scanners, Revision and Tests

10 min read

When you start CS, one of the first problems you will face is not the syllabus. It is information overload. You open YouTube and find twenty teachers explaining the same chapter. You search for classes and find ten academies. Someone recommends one teacher, your friend recommends another, and a senior sends you a third. Then someone tells you to buy a scanner, someone tells you to read the module three times, someone recommends a revision lecture, and someone sends you a PDF of notes. Before you know it, you have collected so much study material that you don't know where to start.

This is one of the biggest traps in professional-course preparation. You think you are preparing to study, but you are actually spending your time researching how to study. There is a point where research itself becomes procrastination. So let me make this chapter simple. Your goal is not to find the perfect combination of teachers, notes, books, scanners and test series. Your goal is to create a study system that works for you and then actually follow it.

Don't choose a class; choose a teacher.

There are hundreds of classes and academies available for CS preparation today. Some are online, some are offline, some are expensive, some are free, some have huge marketing teams, and some are run by one teacher with a small YouTube channel. Don't let the name of the academy make the decision for you. You are not going to spend 100 hours with an academy; you are going to spend those 100 hours with a human being. That person is going to explain the subject to you, influence how you think about it and, in many cases, influence what you notice, remember and eventually understand.

So before paying for a full course, try the teacher. Watch a few lectures from different teachers for the same subject. Don't watch only five minutes. Give each teacher a genuine chance and watch enough to understand their teaching style. See how they explain difficult concepts, whether they simply dictate information or actually make you understand it, whether their pace suits you and whether you can concentrate without constantly checking your phone. Most importantly, ask yourself whether you can explain the concept to yourself after watching the lecture. If you can, you may have found your teacher. If you cannot, keep looking.

You don't have to select the teacher whom everyone else likes. You have to select the teacher with whom you learn best. Someone may tell you, “Bhai, this teacher is the best,” but that does not necessarily mean the teacher is the best for you. The better question is, “Is this teacher the best for me?”

Why does the teacher matter so much?

There is a deeper reason for this. We learn not only from books and written information but also through observation. When you spend 50, 80 or 100 hours listening to the same person explain a subject, that person is not merely transferring information to you. You are repeatedly observing how they think, explain problems, approach difficult concepts and communicate.

Maybe your teacher is extremely organised, curious, patient, analytical or obsessed with accuracy. Maybe they have a particular way of breaking complicated ideas into simple ones. Over time, you may naturally start adopting some of those habits yourself. That is why I don't think choosing a teacher should be treated like choosing a product from Amazon. Choose someone whose way of thinking you wouldn't mind learning from.

There is also a practical reason. You are more likely to give your full attention to someone you connect with. If you like a teacher's personality and teaching style, you naturally become more attentive. If you are constantly irritated by the teacher, even excellent content may struggle to enter your brain. So don't choose a teacher only because someone says they are the best. Choose someone whose teaching makes you want to pay attention and, more importantly, helps you understand.

Explore before choosing, then commit.

This does not mean you should spend six months watching every teacher on the internet. The purpose of exploring different teachers is to make a decision, not to remain permanently undecided. Take one subject, try two or three teachers, watch enough lectures to understand their approach, compare them and then choose one. Once you choose, commit.

One of the biggest mistakes students make is studying one chapter from Teacher A, another from Teacher B, watching a revision lecture from Teacher C and downloading notes from Teacher D. They think they are getting the best of everything, but most of the time they are simply creating confusion. There is enough content available today. Your problem is not a lack of information; your problem is deciding when you have enough information.

Explore before choosing, but once you choose, stop exploring and start studying. Otherwise, you will keep restarting your preparation every time you discover a new teacher or a new method.

Know yourself before choosing your study system.

There is another factor students often ignore: you need to understand your own weaknesses. For example, I personally struggled to make notes while listening to a lecture. I would either listen properly or write properly. Trying to do both often meant that I ended up doing neither particularly well.

So when I selected teachers, I preferred teachers who prepared good notes during the lecture or provided structured notes that I could use later for revision. That small decision made studying much easier for me. This is why I don't believe there is one universal “best study method”.

Your friend may love making handwritten notes, while you may hate it. Someone may learn by reading the module, while someone else may understand only after watching a lecture. Someone may need to solve questions immediately, while someone else may first need conceptual understanding. Know your weaknesses and build your study system around them. Don't copy somebody else's preparation blindly.

What about notes?

Once you select a teacher, use that teacher's notes. You do not need five different sets of notes for the same subject. You don't need one academy's notes, another teacher's handwritten notes, a senior's PDF, a Telegram compilation and a 300-page “ultimate revision book” sitting on your desk. At some point, more material stops being an advantage and becomes noise.

Your teacher's notes, along with the ICSI study material and your own additions, are generally enough to build your preparation around. If your teacher has explained the concept properly and provided usable notes, trust the system. You don't need to keep searching for something better every week.

One thing students often forget is that revision becomes difficult when the material keeps changing. You cannot revise what you keep replacing. If you change your notes every few days, you keep restarting the preparation process. Your goal should be to reach a stage where you have one reliable set of material that you know extremely well. Depth is more useful than volume.

And then comes the scanner.

If you are new to CS, you will probably hear the word “scanner” repeatedly. A scanner is essentially a compilation of questions asked in previous examinations, generally arranged subject-wise or topic-wise. It is useful because it shows you what ICSI has actually asked students in the past.

When you solve a scanner, you are not merely revising. You are doing something much closer to the actual examination. You read a question, recall the concept, understand what the examiner is asking, structure an answer, write it and then compare your answer with the expected approach. That process is far more useful than repeatedly reading the same page and thinking, “Haan haan, ye toh aata hai.”

Knowing something when you read it and being able to produce it when someone asks you a question are two completely different abilities. This is why one of the best forms of revision is to ask yourself questions and answer them honestly. The scanner gives you thousands of opportunities to do exactly that.

Don't read the scanner; solve it.

Many students buy a scanner, highlight important questions, put sticky notes everywhere and then convince themselves that they have revised. But seeing a question is not the same as answering it. You revise when you actually attempt to solve the question without looking at your notes.

You don't have to wait until the entire syllabus is finished. Suppose you complete one chapter. Go to the scanner, find questions from that chapter and try answering them without looking at your notes. You have now started preparing for the examination in a practical way. You are learning how ICSI frames questions, which concepts repeatedly appear, how much detail an answer requires and how to convert your knowledge into an examination answer.

However, don't become dependent on the scanner. It is useful, but it is not the entire syllabus. Don't make the mistake of thinking, “This question has never appeared, so I don't need to study it.” The examiner can ask a completely new question from an old concept. The scanner teaches you the pattern of questioning; it does not guarantee the next question. Use it to understand how concepts are tested and how answers should be framed, but understand your subject first. Concept first, scanner second.

What about revision lectures?

Revision lectures can be extremely useful, particularly when you have already studied the subject once. But don't make them your first exposure to everything. There is a difference between learning and revising.

If you haven't studied a chapter properly and watch a two-hour revision lecture at 1.5x speed, you may feel productive because information is moving quickly. But feeling productive and actually learning are two different things. Use revision lectures to refresh what you already know, identify gaps and bring the subject back into your memory. Then go back to questions.

Ultimately, the examination doesn't ask whether you watched a revision lecture. It asks whether you can answer the question. That should always be the purpose behind your revision.

What about test series?

A test series serves a different purpose. The scanner shows you what has been asked, while a test series shows you how you perform under examination conditions. You need both.

When you take a test, don't judge yourself only by your marks. Look at what went wrong. Did you not know the concept? Did you know it but forget it? Did you misunderstand the question? Did you waste too much time? Did you know the answer but fail to present it properly? Did you write too much? Did you panic?

These questions are much more valuable than simply seeing “52/100” written at the top of your paper. A test is feedback, so use it that way. Your objective is not merely to collect marks in mock tests; it is to identify weaknesses before the real examination exposes them.

And what about friends?

Friends can either make your preparation significantly better or significantly worse. The right study partner can keep you accountable, discuss difficult concepts with you, exchange questions and make the journey less lonely.

The wrong study group can become a WhatsApp group where everyone discusses which teacher is best, which notes are best, how difficult the next attempt will be and whether a particular question is important, while nobody actually studies.

Choose your circle carefully. You don't need ten study partners. You may need only one or two people with whom you can genuinely discuss the subject and who are serious about their preparation.

Also, don't compare your daily progress with everyone around you. Someone will finish the syllabus before you, someone will solve more questions, someone will score more in a test and someone will post their study schedule on Instagram at 5:00 a.m. Good for them. Your job is not to win their preparation race. Your job is to prepare for your examination.

Finally, don't confuse collecting resources with preparation.

This is perhaps the biggest lesson I want you to take from this chapter. You can have the best teacher, the most expensive classes, beautiful notes, five scanners, three test series, ten revision lectures and a WhatsApp group with fifty toppers and still fail if you don't sit down and study.

Resources are tools. They are not preparation.

At some point, you have to close YouTube, close Telegram, put the phone away, open the book, study the concept, ask yourself a question, try to answer it, find what you got wrong and repeat. That is preparation.

If you are confused about which teacher to choose, explore. If you have chosen one, trust them. If you have good notes, stop collecting more. If you have a scanner, solve it. If you have a test series, take the tests. If you have friends, discuss with them. But don't keep changing your system every time somebody tells you that they have found a “better” method.

The best study material is not necessarily the material with the most pages, the most features or the most recommendations. The best study material is the material you actually study. Similarly, the best teacher is not necessarily the teacher with the biggest academy, the most followers or the most famous name. It is the teacher who makes you understand.

Find that person, give them your attention, learn properly and then stop searching. Study, revise, solve and test yourself. Repeat that process consistently.

That's enough. More than enough, actually. Your biggest problem in CS preparation is usually not that you don't have enough resources. It is that you have too many.

6

How to Manage This, Bro?

10 min read

You have realised that there is a small problem nobody properly warned you about: there is a lot to do. You have classes, lectures, books, revision, scanners, tests, college, training or a job, family, friends, health, sleep, maybe a relationship, maybe some ambitions outside CS, and, of course, a phone that is always ready to convince you that watching one more reel is somehow important. At some point, you look at everything you are supposed to do and ask, “How am I supposed to manage all this, bro?”

First, relax. If you feel overwhelmed, it doesn't mean that you are lazy, incapable or not serious enough. It simply means you are trying to fit a lot of responsibilities into a limited amount of time and attention. Almost everyone goes through this.

The problem is that social media has made us believe that disciplined people somehow manage everything perfectly. You see someone studying at 5 a.m., going to the gym, reading books, working, building a business, posting on LinkedIn, spending time with family and sleeping eight hours, and you start thinking that you should be doing all of it too. What you don't see are the compromises, the missed days and the things they had to say no to. You see their highlight reel and compare it with your ordinary Tuesday.

So, before we talk about managing your time, remove one expectation from your mind: you are not going to manage everything perfectly. There will be days when you study brilliantly and days when you barely study. There will be weeks when your schedule works beautifully and weeks when work, college, family or simply life destroys it. That does not mean your system has failed. That is life. The real skill is learning how to continue when things don't go according to plan.

I Tried Almost Everything Before I Figured Out What Worked for Me I personally tried many ways of managing my studies. I made six-month plans, one-month plans and detailed daily schedules. I would decide exactly what I would study, when I would study it and how much I would complete. On paper, everything looked fantastic. In my head, I was basically running a very efficient organisation.

And then reality happened.

One bad day became two. One missed target created another pending target, which made the next day's plan unrealistic. Soon, the beautiful six-month plan became something I avoided because I was already so far behind it.

The problem wasn't that planning was useless. The problem was that I was planning for the person I wanted to be rather than the person I actually was.

Eventually, I found something that worked much better for me: weekly planning. Instead of trying to predict exactly what my life would look like six months later, I would sit down and decide what I realistically wanted to accomplish in the next seven days. More importantly, I deliberately kept the target slightly below what I thought I could do.

If I thought I could finish five chapters, I might plan for three or four. If I thought I could study for thirty hours, I would build the week around a lower number that I knew I could realistically achieve. The idea was not to make the target ridiculously easy. It was to make it achievable even when the week wasn't perfect.

Something interesting started happening. I would finish the planned work earlier than expected, and then I had room to do a little more. I would finish the week feeling that I had succeeded instead of feeling that I had failed. The next week would begin with confidence rather than guilt. Then I would set another realistic target and sometimes exceed it.

Slowly, I created a simple loop: I planned, achieved what I had committed to, felt capable, did a little more when I could and started the next week with confidence. That feeling matters. There is a completely different energy between saying, “I am already ten days behind my plan,” and saying, “I completed everything I planned this week, and I even did a little extra.”

I stopped trying to win the entire six months. I started trying to win the week. Once you learn how to win enough weeks, the months start taking care of themselves.

Don't Build a Plan for Your Fantasy Self This is one of the biggest mistakes students make. You create a timetable assuming that tomorrow you will suddenly become the most disciplined version of yourself. You will wake up early every day, never touch your phone, study for eight hours, exercise, eat perfectly and sleep on time.

Then tomorrow comes, and you are still you. You are tired. You have work. Someone calls you. Traffic happens. You spend forty minutes on your phone. You don't feel like studying. Suddenly, the schedule collapses.

Instead of making a plan that works only when life is perfect, make one that can survive an imperfect week. A six-month goal is useful for direction, but a weekly goal is useful for action. Know where you want to go, but focus on what you need to accomplish next.

You are not required to become a completely different person overnight. You simply need to create a system that the person you are today can actually follow.

And Please, Sleep I know what you're thinking: “Sleep? I have CS to clear.” Exactly. That is why you need sleep.

Students sometimes treat sleep as the first thing to sacrifice when they fall behind. They study until 2 a.m., wake up at 5 a.m., survive on coffee and then proudly tell everyone how little they slept. It sounds disciplined. Sometimes it is simply inefficient.

Sleep is not the opposite of studying. Sleep is part of learning. Research on sleep and memory has repeatedly shown that sleep plays an important role in memory consolidation, helping newly learned information become more stable and easier to retrieve later.That is why I strongly recommend Matthew Walker's Why We Sleep. You don't need to agree with every statement in a book to benefit from reading it, but it changed the way I think about sleep. The important lesson I took from it is simple: sleep is not wasted time. It is part of the biological process that supports learning, memory and performance.

So please don't wear sleep deprivation like a medal. There will be occasional late nights and difficult weeks. That's life. But don't make exhaustion your study strategy. A tired brain sitting in front of a book for six hours is not automatically more productive than a rested brain studying with concentration for three.

My Routine Wasn't Glamorous Either There was a phase of my preparation when my days were honestly exhausting.

I would try to wake up around 5 a.m., at least four days a week. I would make a black coffee, sit down and start studying. On some mornings, I would go straight into lectures and sometimes watch them at 1.5x or even 2x speed, depending on the teacher and the subject. Four hours could disappear into lectures before I even realised it.

Then came office.

Around an hour of travelling in the morning, approximately eight hours at work and another hour and a half or so to get back home. By the time I reached home, I was not exactly fresh. I was cooked. And yet I would try to study for another two or three hours.

Now, before you read
that and think, “Okay,
so this is what I have
to do to clear CS,” please don't. My
routine was my situation, not a formula
for success. Your circumstances may be
completely different. You may have
college, training, family responsibilities or
a completely different energy level.

I am telling you this for a different reason. I want you to understand that having a busy life does not automatically mean that you cannot prepare seriously. You may not have eight free hours every day, but you may have two. You may not be able to study in the morning, but you may be able to study at night. You may not be able to follow someone else's routine, but you can build your own.

The point is not to glorify how much you worked. The point is to show you that you can create pockets of serious effort even when your schedule is already full.

It was not easy for me either.

There were days when I was completely exhausted and days when the last thing I wanted to do was open another lecture.

But somewhere along the way, I started enjoying the process itself. I stopped thinking only about the final result and started enjoying the fact that I was becoming better.

And once you start enjoying the process, something changes. You begin showing up for yourself, not because someone is forcing you or watching you, but because you know that tomorrow's version of you is depending on today's version of you to do the work.

Less Is More Another thing that helped me was learning to reduce the amount of information entering my mind. This sounds strange when you are preparing for a professional examination. You might think that the more you consume, the better prepared you will become. Not necessarily.

You can watch five teachers explain the same chapter, read three sets of notes, follow ten Telegram channels, save fifty revision videos and still not remember what you studied yesterday. At some point, more information becomes interference.

Once I had selected my teacher and my study material, I tried to restrict myself to information that was actually relevant to my preparation. If I was studying one subject, I didn't need to know what every other teacher on the internet was saying about it. If I had good notes, I didn't need another PDF simply because someone forwarded it to me. If I had a scanner, I didn't need five more compilations of previous questions.

You have limited attention, so protect it. The internet gives you unlimited information, but your brain doesn't have unlimited attention. When you are preparing for an examination, you don't need to know everything that exists about a subject. You need to understand what matters and be able to reproduce it when you are asked.

Use the Time You Already Have One of the easiest ways to find additional time is to stop thinking that learning can happen only when you are sitting at a desk.

For example, while travelling, I would sometimes listen to voice notes or revision material. For ESG, I remember listening to voice notes from Atal by Chirag Sir while travelling. I also used to record random voice notes to myself on WhatsApp—sometimes a concept I had just learned, sometimes something I knew I would forget later—and listen to those recordings again when I had time.

It wasn't some sophisticated productivity system. It was simply making use of otherwise unused time.

If you spend an hour travelling every day, that doesn't mean you can turn that entire hour into deep study. Don't fool yourself into thinking you can solve a difficult numerical or write a full examination answer while standing in traffic. But perhaps you can listen to a revision lecture, recall a concept or listen to your own voice explaining something.

At the same time, don't feel that every minute of your day must be productive. Sometimes you need to rest. The point is not to squeeze every possible second out of your life until you hate it. The point is to be intentional with the time you have.

When It Gets Hard and Boring, Remember Why You're Doing It There will be days when studying becomes incredibly hard and boring.

You have been reading for an hour, the chapter doesn't seem to end, you have read the same provision twice and your phone is sitting next to you.

Suddenly, checking Instagram feels like an urgent responsibility.

When that happens, I sometimes ask myself a slightly stupid but surprisingly effective question: “If this were a movie and I were the main character, what would I be doing right now?”

I imagine myself sitting there, tired, surrounded by books, trying to finish one more chapter while everyone else is sleeping or enjoying themselves. I think, “This is the part of the movie nobody puts in the trailer.”

Nobody celebrates the boring Tuesday night. Nobody makes a motivational reel about the third hour of studying when your brain has stopped cooperating. But if this were a story, this would probably be the scene where the character is being built.

The struggle rarely looks impressive while you are inside it. It looks impressive only when you look backwards.

So when studying feels boring, don't always ask yourself whether you feel like doing it. Ask yourself what the person you want to become would do in that moment. Then do that.

7

Decide What Is Enough?

10 min read

Why do we never feel like we have done enough?

Have you ever finished studying a chapter and instead of feeling satisfied, immediately thought, “Maybe I should study it one more time”? You finish your target for the day, but then you see someone studying for another two hours and suddenly your own effort feels insufficient. You complete the syllabus, but now you think you should read another book. You solve the scanner, but then someone sends you another question bank. You watch your teacher's revision lecture, but then another teacher uploads a “complete revision” video and you start wondering whether you missed something. This is one of the strangest problems students face during professional courses: there is always something more you can do. And because there is always something more, you can keep working indefinitely without ever feeling that you have actually finished.

So before asking yourself how much more you should study, ask a much more important question: what exactly am I trying to achieve? If you don't know the destination, you cannot know when you have travelled far enough. This is where the idea of teleology becomes useful. Don't let the word scare you; it simply refers to understanding something in relation to its purpose or end goal. Your preparation has to be connected to the purpose for which you are preparing. If the purpose is to clear the CS examination, your preparation should ultimately be designed around clearing the examination. If your purpose is to score exceptionally high, your definition of enough will naturally be different. If your purpose is to become an expert in a particular area for your future career, that is again a different goal. The same chapter can therefore require different amounts of effort depending on what you are trying to achieve.

But why does having a goal make such a difference?

Our mind is not just a machine that receives information; it is constantly trying to move towards something. We set targets, compare our current position with where we want to be, receive feedback and adjust our behaviour. This is one of the ideas explored, in a broader and somewhat metaphorical way, by Maxwell Maltz in Psycho-Cybernetics. The book presents the mind as a goal-oriented mechanism that can be directed towards a chosen objective. Whether or not you agree with every idea in the book, the framework is extremely useful for a student. Give yourself a destination and your brain has something to work towards. Don't give yourself a destination and you can keep moving without knowing whether you are actually making progress.

That is exactly why the weekly planning method I discussed in the previous chapter worked for me. I don't want you to decide that you have to study ten hours every day for the next six months. Decide what you want to accomplish this week. If you complete that target, you have achieved something measurable. You know where you stand. You can then decide the next target. It sounds simple, but psychologically it feels very different from living under a permanent feeling of “I am behind.”

What happened when I started planning only for the week?

I had tried almost everything before arriving at this. I made six-month plans. I made one-month plans. I made detailed schedules where I had practically decided what I would study on every particular day. The plans looked fantastic when I made them. The problem was that I was planning for a version of myself who apparently had no bad days, no unexpected work, no tiredness and no life outside studying.

Then reality would happen. I would miss one target. That target would get pushed to the next day. The next day's target was already full, so now I was behind by two things. Then another day would go badly. Eventually, the beautiful plan became another reason to feel guilty. I wasn't necessarily studying less; I was simply spending too much mental energy thinking about everything I had failed to complete.

Then I started working with weekly targets. I would decide what I realistically wanted to complete in the next seven days. I deliberately preferred a target that was slightly under what I thought I could theoretically accomplish. Not ridiculously easy, but achievable even if the week wasn't perfect. Something interesting started happening. I would often complete the target before the week ended, and because I had some energy left, I would sometimes do a little extra. More importantly, I would end the week with the feeling that I won.

That created a small loop: I set a target, I achieved it, I felt capable, I started the next week with more confidence, and then I repeated it. I wasn't trying to win six months anymore. I was trying to win one week. And when you win enough weeks, the six months start taking care of themselves.

So if I finish my weekly target early, should I stop?

Yes. And I want you to understand why I am saying this because it goes against everything we are normally taught as ambitious students. Suppose you planned three chapters, solved the relevant questions and took your test, and somehow you finished everything by Saturday morning. If you genuinely want to study more, go ahead. There is absolutely nothing wrong with doing extra work. But if you have completed your target and are now sitting with a feeling of guilt because you think, “I still have Saturday and Sunday, so I should probably do something else,” then stop for a moment. You are allowed to relax.

You are allowed to enjoy your Saturday.

You are allowed to meet your friends, watch a movie, go out, sleep, play a game or simply do nothing. You don't have to immediately create another mountain just because you reached the one you originally decided to climb. You need to allow yourself to experience completion. That small feeling of achievement matters. When you repeatedly set realistic targets and actually achieve them, you start building evidence that you can trust yourself. That is far more useful than constantly moving the finish line and living with the feeling that you are never doing enough.

But isn't doing more always better?

No. This is one of the biggest traps in professional-course preparation. More information is not always more knowledge, and more hours are not always more preparation. Imagine you have ten important topics in front of you. You spend three days mastering the first topic so deeply that you can practically teach it to someone else, but by the end of those three days you have barely touched the other nine. You may feel extremely knowledgeable, but are you actually better prepared for the examination? Probably not.

This is why I don't want you to become a perfectionist in your CS preparation. The examination does not reward you for knowing one chapter at an extraordinary depth while the rest of the syllabus remains untouched. You first need reasonable command over the breadth of the syllabus and then deeper preparation in the areas that deserve it. There is a difference between wanting to understand something properly and refusing to stop until you know absolutely everything about it. The first is excellence. The second can become perfectionism.

Look at the examination for what it actually is. Your objective is not to become the world's leading expert on every provision you read during your CS preparation. Your objective is to develop the level of knowledge required to answer the examination and, eventually, to become a competent professional. Even ICSI's study material distinguishes between different levels of knowledge expected in different parts of the curriculum. If the requirement for a particular area is working knowledge, don't create a personal requirement of becoming an expert in it simply because you are afraid of leaving something out. If something genuinely requires deeper understanding, give it the time it deserves. Know what is required before deciding how much effort is required.

How do I know whether I am preparing enough?

Look at the goal, not your anxiety. Ask yourself whether you have understood the concepts, whether you can recall them, whether you can answer the questions being asked, whether you have covered the relevant syllabus and whether your preparation is at the level expected by the Institute. Look at previous-year questions. Listen to the teacher you have chosen. Use the scanner to understand how questions are framed. These things give you feedback about your actual preparation. What you should not use as your measurement is somebody else's study hours. Your friend may study twelve hours. Another person may study six. Someone may revise five times. Someone else may revise twice and still perform better because their first two revisions were more effective. Hours are an input; the examination result is an output. Don't become obsessed with the input while ignoring whether the output is improving.

What if everyone around me is doing more?

This is where another book becomes relevant: The Courage to Be Disliked by Ichiro Kishimi and Fumitake Koga. One of the ideas that stayed with me from the book is the importance of separating your own responsibilities and goals from the expectations of other people. You don't have to live according to somebody else's definition of success.

During CS, you will constantly hear what other people are doing. “I studied twelve hours.” “I completed three revisions.” “I watched this teacher.” “I solved ten papers.” “I am targeting ninety.” And suddenly their preparation becomes your benchmark. You start increasing your workload not because your goal requires it, but because someone else made you feel inadequate.

You need the courage to say, “That may be enough for you. I need to decide what is enough for me.” This doesn't mean ignoring advice or becoming careless. It means understanding your own goal, your own circumstances and your own capacity. You are responsible for your preparation. Someone else's study schedule cannot sit for your examination.

Isn't this just an excuse to study less?

It can be, if you misuse it. “Enough” should never become an excuse for laziness. If you planned three chapters because you wanted to avoid studying and then call it a realistic target, you are fooling yourself. The whole philosophy works only when the target itself is honest. You have to be ambitious enough to demand genuine effort from yourself and realistic enough to make the target achievable. There is a difference between “I have done enough” and “I don't feel like doing more.” Sometimes you have done enough. Sometimes you are simply tired and looking for an excuse. You have to be brutally honest with yourself about which one it is. That is why your weekly target should be decided before you start the week, not after you become tired on Sunday night. Decide in advance what would make you say, “Yes, I genuinely worked this week.” Then hold yourself accountable to it. Once you have done it, give yourself permission to stop.

Why do I keep saying that you should sometimes slow down?

Because you cannot ride a bike towards a destination with the accelerator permanently pressed at maximum. At some point, you have to slow down. Sometimes you have to stop. Sometimes you need to get off the bike, breathe, look around and realise how far you have already travelled.

Your CS journey is not a three-month sprint. It is a professional qualification that requires sustained effort. If you spend the entire journey operating at maximum intensity, you may reach the next milestone exhausted and then have nothing left for the one after it. There will be periods when you have to push extremely hard, especially close to examinations. But pushing hard is useful only when you can recover and continue.

You are not a machine.

And even machines need maintenance.

So what should “enough” actually mean for a CS student?

Enough should mean enough for the goal you have set. It should be based on what the examination requires, what your teacher expects, what your current level is and what you need to improve. It should not be decided by fear, comparison or the endless availability of more material.

If you have genuinely achieved the target you set for the week, celebrate the win. If you have covered the required breadth of the syllabus and can answer the relevant questions, don't spend another three days perfecting one small topic just because you are scared of moving on. If you have studied properly for the day, you don't have to feel guilty for closing the book.

There will always be another lecture. Another revision. Another question. Another book. Another person telling you that you should be doing more.

You cannot spend your entire journey with the accelerator pressed to the floor simply because you are afraid that slowing down means falling behind.

Know your destination. Understand what the destination requires. Work seriously towards it. And when you have reached the target you set, have the courage to breathe.

Because sometimes the most productive thing you can say to yourself is not “I can do more.”

It is:
