“I have done what I needed to do. That's enough for today.”
8

How to Go All In?

18 min read

What happens when there is only one month left?

There comes a point in every CS student's journey when all the normal rules change. Until now, you were trying to manage everything together. You were studying along with college, training, work, family, friends and everything else life was throwing at you. You were attending lectures when you could, revising when you could, making notes when you could and somehow trying to keep the entire thing moving. But then suddenly you look at the calendar and realise that there are only thirty days left. Or twenty. Or ten. And suddenly the question is no longer, “How do I balance everything?” The question becomes, “How do I use whatever time is left?”

And this is where I want to tell you something very clearly: in the final stretch, you have no choice but to go all in. Not because studying twelve or fourteen hours a day is some magical formula. Not because suffering makes you more deserving of success. And certainly not because you have to prove to someone that you are serious. You go all in because the examination is now so close that there is simply no room left for the normal version of your life. Your lectures may still be incomplete. Your revision may not be finished. Your handwritten notes may be half-made. There may be chapters you haven't touched. You may not feel confident. You may look at your preparation and think, “How am I going to finish all this?” Welcome to the final month.

I know exactly what that feels like.

Why does the last month feel so different?

Because this is the final round of the marathon. Imagine running a long-distance race and reaching the last few kilometres. You don't suddenly become a different human being, but your behaviour changes because the finish line is finally visible. The problem is that students often make one of two mistakes here. Some panic so badly that they keep changing their strategy, downloading new material, watching new teachers and creating new plans. Others become so overwhelmed by the amount left that they mentally give up before the examination has even arrived.

Don't do either.

The last month is not the time to redesign your entire preparation. It is the time to execute what you already have. You have whatever lectures you have watched. You have whatever notes you have made. You have your study material. You have the scanner. You have your previous preparation. Now you need to extract as much as possible from what is already on your table.

This is where I personally became almost obsessive.

What did I actually do when my examination came close?

Before my examination, I told both of my trainers—first during my training at a firm and later during my training in a listed company— that I was going to take a full thirty days of leave for examination preparation. Looking back, I still feel slightly guilty about it because I knew thirty days was a significant amount of time to be away from work. But I also knew what I needed at that point. I needed uninterrupted time.

And once that leave started, I went into something very close to isolation.

I removed social media. I didn't want notifications, reels, messages, random opinions or somebody else's preparation appearing on my screen every ten minutes. I prepared my notes and material in advance. I decided that I wasn't going to keep hunting for new resources. I was going to eat what was already on my table.

That sentence sounds funny, but it became a rule for me. I didn't need another teacher.

I didn't need another PDF.

I didn't need another “last 10 days strategy.” I needed to finish what I already had.

My room started looking less like a bedroom and more like a command centre. I would stick notes around me. Sometimes I would literally write things on the wall. My mother got quite irritated with me because, understandably, she didn't particularly enjoy seeing the walls covered with my study material. I remember telling her, “I'll get this painted. Just let me do what I need to do right now.” That was the mindset.

I wasn't trying to make my preparation look organised anymore. I was trying to execute it.

And there is a difference.

Does “going all in” mean studying like a maniac?

For the final stretch, your intensity will probably look slightly crazy to someone outside your situation.

Your friends may ask why you are not meeting them. Your family may wonder why you are sitting with books all day. Someone may message you and think you are ignoring them. You may disappear from social media.

You may stop going out.

Your room may become a mess.

Your schedule may look completely different from normal life. And honestly, that's okay for a limited period. You know what you are doing.

There is a difference between being irresponsible and temporarily becoming extremely focused because you have a specific deadline. If you have ten days left before an examination, this is not the time to maintain your normal entertainment schedule simply because “balance is important.” The examination is ten days away. The priority is obvious.

But remember: going all in is temporary intensity, not a permanent lifestyle.

You don't need to live like this for a year. You need to use the final available days intelligently.

But what if studying becomes incredibly boring?

Now we come to the real enemy.

Not the syllabus.

Not the examination.

Not even the lack of time.

Boredom.

Because eventually you have to sit there and read the same subject again. You have already watched the lecture. You have already highlighted the material. You have already read the provision. And now the thought of looking at it again feels unbearable.

This is where you need to understand something about attention. Your brain does not automatically give equal attention to everything. Novelty naturally attracts attention. Something new feels interesting because your brain has a reason to investigate it. This is one reason students suddenly become extremely interested in a new teacher's revision video when they are supposed to be revising their existing notes. New teacher. New voice. New slides. New explanation. It feels productive because it feels fresh.

But fresh is not the same as useful.

The final month is where you have to fight that temptation.

You have to make the familiar interesting.

So how do you make boring revision interesting?

Change the way you interact with the information. If you have already read a chapter five times, don't simply read it for the sixth time. Ask yourself questions. Close the book and try to recall the provisions. Take a blank sheet and write everything you remember. Explain the concept aloud as if you are teaching someone. Try predicting what question could be asked. Look at the heading and attempt to reconstruct the answer before opening the page. Solve the previous-year question without looking at the solution. Suddenly, revision stops being passive.

You are no longer staring at information.

You are trying to retrieve it.

And this matters because research on learning consistently finds that retrieval practice—actively trying to recall information rather than simply rereading it—can produce stronger long-term learning than passive rereading. This is one of the reasons the scanner becomes so powerful during the final stage. It doesn't just tell you what has been asked; it forces you to confront the question: “Can I actually produce this answer?”

That little moment when you close the book and struggle to remember something is not evidence that studying isn't working. That struggle is part of the learning.

What if I know the answer when I see it but can't write it myself?

This is exactly why you should stop confusing recognition with recall. You read a provision and think, “Yes, yes, I know this.” Then someone asks you to explain it without the book. Silence. You look at the answer and immediately think, “Oh yes, I knew that!” No, you recognised it.

There is a difference.

The examination doesn't put the answer in front of you and ask whether it looks familiar. It asks you to produce something from your own memory.

So during the last month, don't spend all your time making the page look familiar.

Practise making your brain produce the answer. That means questions.

That means scanners.

That means writing.

That means speaking the answer aloud.

That means closing the book and testing yourself. The more you make your brain retrieve information, the more comfortable the actual examination environment becomes.

Why am I telling you to restrict information again?

Because in the final month, information overload can destroy your preparation.

Imagine you have thirty days left and suddenly discover a new teacher who has uploaded a fifty-hour “complete revision.” You watch two hours. Now you feel that your existing notes are incomplete. You download another PDF. Someone sends you a new question bank. Another person recommends another book. Your Telegram groups are full of predictions about what will come in the examination. And suddenly you are surrounded by information but moving nowhere.

Stop.

Your table already contains enough.

Your job is not to consume the entire internet before the examination. Your job is to make what you already know exam-ready. This is why I made a very deliberate decision during my final preparation: no unnecessary new material. I had already chosen my sources. I had my notes. I had my study material. I had my questions. I was going to finish those first.

Think of your preparation like eating.

If you have a full plate of food in front of you, finding another restaurant isn't going to help you.

Eat the food already on the plate.

Only after that should you worry about whether you need anything else.

Can small things actually make a difference?

Absolutely.

When you are studying for long hours, small environmental decisions become surprisingly important. Keep water next to you instead of repeatedly getting up to find it. A simple two-litre bottle or even a large tumbler costs very little but removes unnecessary interruptions. Keep your stationery ready. Keep your books arranged before you begin. Decide what you are studying before you sit down. Keep your phone away rather than negotiating with yourself every five minutes about whether you should check it.

These things sound almost too small to mention. But that is the point.

You don't need a revolutionary productivity hack. Sometimes you just need to remove twenty tiny reasons to get distracted.

If your phone is in another room, you don't need willpower every thirty seconds.

If your water is beside you, you don't need to get up repeatedly. If your notes are already arranged, you don't spend ten minutes searching for them.

If tomorrow's chapter is already decided tonight, you don't waste your first twenty minutes deciding what to study. Good preparation reduces the number of decisions you have to make.

What about coffee, music, lights and all those little study hacks? Use whatever genuinely helps you focus, but don't turn studying into a ritual so complicated that you cannot study without it. You don't need a ₹5,000 study lamp, a special notebook, a particular playlist and a productivity app before you can open the Companies Act.

During my preparation, black coffee was sometimes enough to signal to my brain, “Okay, we're working now.” That doesn't mean coffee magically creates discipline. It simply became part of my routine. The same applies to your study environment. Find a place where you can concentrate. Keep it reasonably clean. Keep your materials accessible. Make the default action the action you want to take. The goal is simple:

Make studying easier to start and harder to interrupt.

What if I still don't feel confident?

Let me tell you something that nobody likes to admit during exam preparation: you may never feel completely ready. You may finish your revision and still feel that you have forgotten half of what you studied. You may open a chapter you studied two months ago and suddenly wonder whether you ever studied it at all. You may take a mock test and score much lower than you expected, and for the next few hours your brain will start telling you that everyone else is prepared except you. I have been there. And if you are there right now, don't panic. That feeling does not necessarily mean you are unprepared; sometimes it simply means you are finally close enough to the examination for the uncertainty to feel real. I used to think confidence had to come first. I thought one day I would finish enough revision, look at my books and suddenly feel, “Yes, now I am ready.” That day rarely comes. What actually happens is much less dramatic. You study, you test yourself, you discover that you don't remember something, you go back and fix it, you test yourself again, and slowly you start noticing that the things which scared you last week are becoming easier. Confidence is often not the starting point of preparation; it is the result of preparation. So don't sit around waiting to feel confident before you work. Work until your confidence has a reason to exist. If you don't remember something, revise it. If you can't answer a question, learn how to answer it. If your mock test goes badly, find out why. Don't turn every weakness into an identity crisis. A gap in your preparation is a gap to be fixed, not proof that you cannot clear the examination.

So what does “going all in” actually mean?

Going all in does not mean destroying yourself or trying to prove how many hours you can sit with a book. It means that, for a short and clearly defined period, you remove everything that does not deserve priority anymore. If you have thirty days left, the examination has to become the dominant priority of those thirty days. Social media can wait. Parties can wait. Random courses can wait. Learning another skill can wait. New books can wait. Unnecessary conversations can wait. Even some work responsibilities may need to be temporarily reduced if you have the ability to take leave. You are not giving up your life. You are simply narrowing it for a little while. I did exactly that. Before my examination, I told my trainers that I wanted to take thirty days of leave for preparation. Once I got that time, I didn't want to use it to maintain my normal lifestyle and somehow squeeze studying into the gaps. I wanted to create a gap in normal life and fill it with preparation. Social media went out. Unnecessary distractions went out. My material was already arranged. I wasn't interested in discovering a new teacher or downloading another PDF every second day. I had decided what I was going to study, and my job was to finish it.

That period probably looked slightly ridiculous from the outside. My room had notes stuck everywhere. I would write things down wherever I thought they might help me remember them. At one point, my mother was understandably quite irritated because I had started writing directly on the walls. I remember telling her, in essence, “I'll get it painted later. Just let me do what I need to do right now.” It wasn't some perfectly aesthetic study setup. It was messy, obsessive and sometimes completely exhausting. But I wasn't trying to create a picture of a productive student. I was trying to become one.

What if I only have twenty days left? Or ten?

Then you have twenty days. Or ten. That's it. Don't spend the first three of them emotionally negotiating with the calendar. I have seen students lose valuable days simply thinking about how many days they have already wasted. They calculate what they could have completed if they had started earlier, compare themselves with someone who finished the syllabus two months ago and then spend another evening worrying about whether they can still do it. None of that adds a single mark to your answer sheet.

If you have twenty days, ask what can realistically be done in twenty days. If you have ten, ask what can be done in ten. At this stage, preparation needs to become brutally practical. Revise the important material. Solve questions. Use the scanner. Identify the areas where you repeatedly make mistakes. Practise writing answers. Go back to the provisions and concepts you keep forgetting. Test yourself. Fix the gaps. Repeat. Don't suddenly conclude that because you have less time, you need more material. You don't need more information; you need more execution.

There is a very common panic response in the final days: “Maybe I should start watching this teacher's revision series.” Then another teacher. Then another PDF. Then someone's handwritten notes. Then a new test series. Before you realise it, you have spent two days collecting resources instead of revising. Don't do that. Your final days should be about extracting maximum value from what you already have, not constantly searching for something that will magically rescue your preparation.

But how do I make myself study when revision has become unbearably boring?

This is where you have to stop expecting studying to entertain you. Some parts of CS are simply boring. There is no motivational quote that is going to make every provision of every law fascinating. But there is a difference between boring information and boring studying. You can change how you interact with the information. If you have read a chapter five times, don't simply read it a sixth time. Close the book and ask yourself what you remember. Take a blank sheet and reconstruct the answer. Look at a question from the scanner and try to answer it before seeing the solution. Explain the concept aloud as if someone has just asked you about it. Try to predict what your examiner could ask from that chapter. Suddenly your brain is no longer passively looking at familiar words; it is being forced to retrieve something.

That matters because your examination will not ask, “Does this answer look familiar to you?” It will ask you to produce the answer yourself. Recognition feels comfortable, but recall is what you actually need in the examination hall. So when revision feels difficult because you can't immediately remember something, don't always interpret that difficulty as failure. Sometimes the struggle to retrieve is exactly the exercise your memory needs.

I used to record videos of myself teaching and post them on YouTube. I wasn't trying to create content. I didn't make thumbnails, write captions or edit anything. I would simply open my phone and start teaching. It felt awkward in the beginning, but it created accountability. Eventually, the process became interesting. And if I didn't record a video, I recorded my voice and sent it to myself on WhatsApp. I even created groups named CRVI, CRI, ESG, CMADD and one for each subject. Whenever I needed to revise, I would play those recordings while doing other work.

It wasn't polished. It wasn't meant for an audience. It was just another way of forcing myself to recall what I had studied. I couldn't hide behind familiar-looking notes when I was speaking. I had to explain the concept clearly, and the moment I got stuck, I knew exactly what I had failed to understand.

That is the point. You don't need to create perfect revision content.

You need to create accountability.

Record yourself. Explain the topic aloud. Send the recording to yourself. Play it while walking or doing something routine. Do whatever forces your brain to produce the answer instead of merely recognising it on the page.

Why does the final phase sometimes start feeling strangely exciting?

Because once you stop negotiating with yourself, something changes. In the beginning, sitting down for six hours can feel impossible. But after a few days of serious focus, you start seeing progress everywhere. A chapter disappears. Then another. A question that confused you yesterday becomes easy today. You take a test and recognise the pattern of a question. You remember a provision without opening the book. Your revision starts connecting with your earlier preparation.

And slowly, the work itself starts giving you a reward. That is what happened to me. I was tired, sometimes completely exhausted, but there were moments when I genuinely enjoyed the feeling of seeing the preparation come together. I wasn't enjoying every chapter. I wasn't suddenly in love with studying. I was enjoying getting better. That distinction matters.

You don't have to love the activity every minute. You can learn to love the evidence that the activity is working. There is something deeply satisfying about sitting down with a topic you couldn't answer a week ago and answering it correctly today. That is progress you can feel. And once you start seeing that progress, you don't need someone constantly shouting at you to study. You start showing up because you want to see yourself improve again.

What if people around me think I have gone crazy?

They probably will.

And honestly, during the final few weeks, you may look slightly crazy from the outside. Your friends may wonder why you disappeared. Your family may wonder why you are sitting with books all day. Someone may message you and ask why you are not replying. Your social media may go completely silent. Your room may be full of notes. Your conversations may somehow turn into provisions, sections, questions and examination dates.

That's okay.

They are looking at your life from the outside. You know the deadline. If you have deliberately decided to take thirty days away from work or reduce your social life because you want to give your examination your best shot, that is not something you need to apologise for. You are allowed to be unusually focused for an unusually short period when there is an unusually important goal in front of you. But remember the words short period. Going all in is not an instruction to permanently neglect your health, relationships or life. It is a temporary narrowing of your attention. There will be time for everything else again. There will be friends after the examination. There will be work after the examination. There will be weekends after the examination. There will be sleep after the examination. Right now, you have this particular window. Use it.

What should I do when my brain keeps telling me I am not ready?

Stop having that conversation.

Not because the thought isn't real, but because it isn't useful anymore. Maybe you are not ready. Fine. Then become more ready. Maybe you could have prepared better. Obviously. Almost everyone could have. Maybe somebody else has studied more. Probably. None of those facts tell you what to do with the next hour.

The final days are not the time to keep asking whether you should have started earlier. You can't go back. They are not the time to wonder whether someone else is ahead of you. You can't control that either. And they are certainly not the time to redesign your entire strategy every morning.

Ask one question: “What can I do with the time I have left?” Then do that. If the answer is one chapter, study the chapter. If it is fifty questions, solve the fifty questions. If it is a revision of provisions you keep forgetting, revise them. If it is a mock test, take it. If you are exhausted and your brain genuinely needs sleep, sleep and come back. Don't turn preparation into a philosophical debate every morning. At some point, thinking about preparation has to stop and preparation has to begin.

9

What to Do Just Before the Exam?

4 min read

So, finally, the day has come. The books are closed, the last revision is done—or maybe it isn't, because let's be honest, you will probably find something to revise even five minutes before leaving for the examination centre. You have spent months thinking about this day, and now suddenly it is sitting right in front of you. And strangely, this is where your brain can become your biggest enemy. You may suddenly remember the one chapter you didn't revise properly. You may hear that someone has completed five revisions. You may open your notes “just for ten minutes” and end up jumping from one topic to another. You may start searching for important questions on WhatsApp or Telegram. Please don't do that. The examination is no longer the time to build preparation. It is the time to trust the preparation you have built.

The night before the examination, your job is not to become a different student. You are not going to learn an entire subject overnight. You are certainly not going to become an expert at 2 a.m. What you can do is protect what you already have. Keep your admit card and whatever you need ready. Keep your stationery ready. Know where your examination centre is. Set your alarm. Eat something sensible. Drink enough water. And most importantly, sleep. I know, I know—you are thinking, “Bro, how can I sleep when I still have so much left?” You sleep because tomorrow your brain has to retrieve everything you spent months putting into it. A tired brain is not a badge of honour. You don't get bonus marks for reaching the examination hall looking like you haven't slept since the previous attempt. And if you haven't finished everything, accept it. Seriously. Accept it. There is always going to be something left. Maybe you didn't revise that last chapter. Maybe your handwritten notes are incomplete. Maybe you wanted to solve one more paper. Maybe you still don't feel confident. Fine. The preparation is imperfect. Your job now is to extract the maximum marks possible from that imperfect preparation. Don't turn an incomplete chapter into an incomplete attempt. Don't let the fact that you haven't studied everything make you forget everything you have studied.

This is also the time to stop consuming other people's anxiety. If your friend calls you at 11 p.m. and says, “Bro, have you done Chapter 14? Sir said it is very important,” don't suddenly throw away your entire plan. If somebody sends you a PDF titled “Most Important 50 Questions Guaranteed for Tomorrow,” remember that the person who created that PDF does not have access to the question paper sitting inside the examination authority's system. Relax. You don't need a prediction. You need preparation.

And then comes the morning. You wake up, get ready and for a few minutes you may feel completely normal. Then, somewhere between breakfast and reaching the centre, your heart starts beating a little faster. That's normal too. Don't interpret nervousness as a sign that you are going to fail. Your body understands that something important is about to happen. Let it happen. Take a few deep breaths. Walk slowly. Don't sit outside the centre discussing the syllabus with ten other students. That last-minute conversation has almost never ended with someone saying, “You know what, I feel much more peaceful now.”

If you have a teacher whose lectures genuinely helped you, this is a beautiful moment to remember them with gratitude. Not because they can write the paper for you, but because somewhere during the last few months, someone sat in front of a camera or in a classroom and explained something that you eventually understood. Think about that. You started with confusion. Then someone explained it. You practised it. You revised it. And now you are carrying that knowledge into the examination hall. Be grateful. I personally like looking back at the teachers whose lectures I studied from and thinking, “Sir, ma'am, ab aapka kaam khatam. Ab meri baari hai.”

And then, just before you enter the examination hall, tell yourself something very simple: “I don't need to know everything. I just need to answer what I know, correctly and calmly.”

You have already done the hard part. You woke up when you didn't want to. You attended lectures when they felt boring. You revised when you wanted to scroll. You solved questions when you wanted to quit. You sat through those final days when everyone else seemed to be living normally. You gave up things. You made mistakes. You came back. You kept showing up. So now stop asking yourself whether you are ready. Maybe you are. Maybe you aren't. It doesn't matter anymore.

“The preparation is over. The performance begins now.”

10

What to Do During the Exam?

4 min read

Now you are sitting in the examination hall. The paper is in your hands. For months you imagined this moment, and now it is almost strangely ordinary. A clock is ticking. Someone is adjusting their chair. Somebody is already turning pages like they have received the question paper three years ago. And your brain is saying, “What if I don't know anything?”

Relax.

Read the paper.

That's it.

Don't decide your result in the first five minutes. Sometimes the first question will be beautiful and familiar. Sometimes it will be something you weren't expecting. Sometimes you will turn the page and think, “What the hell is this?” That reaction is not a result. It is just a reaction. Don't let one unfamiliar question convince you that the entire examination has gone against you. There are marks scattered across that paper, and your job is to collect them.

Read the questions carefully. Understand what is actually being asked. Don't start writing simply because you recognise the topic. If the question asks you to explain something, explain it. If it asks for provisions, give the provisions. If it asks for a distinction, make a distinction. If it asks for an application, apply the concept. Answer the question that is on the paper, not the question you wish they had asked.

And please don't fall in love with one question. Sometimes students see a question they know extremely well and become so excited that they spend half an hour writing everything they have ever learned about the topic. Congratulations, you have just written a PhD thesis for a five-mark question. Move on. Marks matter, and time matters. Give an answer the time it deserves.

If you get stuck on a question, don't sit there staring at it as though the answer is going to appear through telepathy. Give it a reasonable attempt, mark it if necessary and move forward. You may remember the answer twenty minutes later. The human brain is strange like that. Sometimes the answer comes to you while you are writing another question. Let it.

And if you suddenly realise that you don't know an answer, don't panic. You are not expected to know everything. Your paper is not going to be judged against an imaginary perfect student who knew every question. It is going to be judged on what you actually write. So use what you know. Apply concepts. Structure your answer. Use headings where appropriate. Write relevant provisions. Give examples if they genuinely help. Make your answer easy for the examiner to follow.

Most importantly, don't allow another student's speed to become your problem. You will hear pages turning. You will see somebody asking for extra sheets. You may look at the clock and think, “Everyone is writing more than me.” Ignore it. You have absolutely no idea whether the person sitting three seats away is writing brilliant answers or simply writing a lot of words.

You are not competing with the sound of someone else's pen. You are competing with the question paper.

And there may be a moment when the paper feels terrible. Maybe the questions are not what you expected. Maybe your favourite chapter didn't come. Maybe the paper is harder than your mock tests. At that moment, remember something important: a difficult paper is difficult for everyone. Don't waste fifteen minutes emotionally reacting to it.

Adjust. If the paper has become difficult, your strategy has to become calmer.

This is where all those boring mock tests suddenly become useful. You have already experienced the feeling of being stuck. You have already made mistakes. You have already practised managing time. Now use that experience.

And if you make a silly mistake, don't let one mistake become five. You may realise halfway through the paper that you misunderstood one question. Fine. Correct your approach and continue. The examination does not end because you made one mistake.

There is also something philosophical about the examination hall that I want you to remember. You cannot control the paper anymore. You cannot control which chapter appears. You cannot control the examiner's mood. You cannot control what your friend is writing. You cannot control what you remembered yesterday and forgot today. You can control one thing:

The next answer.

So stay there. Answer the next question.

Then the next.

Then the next.

Don't write the entire three-hour paper in your head before you start. Just play the next ball.

If you have watched enough cricket, you have heard the phrase: “One ball at a time.” It sounds cliché until you are actually under pressure. Then it becomes incredibly useful. Don't worry about question number 20 while you are answering question number 4. Don't worry about the result while you are still writing the paper.

Your only job is to make the next answer better. And when the last fifteen or twenty minutes arrive, become practical. Don't start writing unnecessary material just because you are nervous.

Check what you can realistically check. Make sure you haven't missed a question. Complete what you can. Manage your remaining time intelligently.

Then, when the invigilator says, “Stop writing,” stop. Don't keep calculating marks in your head.

Don't immediately start comparing answers.

Don't walk outside and ask ten people, “What did you write for Question 3?”

Just breathe.

You survived the paper. Whatever happened, happened. And you still have another paper in the future if you are appearing for multiple papers.

Don't let one examination steal the next one from you. You came into the hall carrying months of preparation. Now leave carrying one thing: the knowledge that you gave that paper your best shot with what you had.

That's enough. For now.

11

What to Do Just After the Exams?

6 min read

And then suddenly, it's over.

You walk out of the examination centre, and something strange happens. The thing that occupied your mind for months is no longer sitting in front of you. No more chapters, no more revision targets, no more waking up thinking about the next paper. For a few seconds, you may feel amazing. You have finally finished the paper you were worrying about for weeks.

Then someone walks out behind you and says, “Bhai, Question 5 mein kya likha?”Please keep walking.

I am serious. The post-examination discussion is one of the most useless rituals students have invented. You compare answers, someone says you are wrong, another person says the examiner will definitely give marks, someone starts calculating the expected score, and within twenty minutes, you have gone from “I think the paper went okay” to “Bhai, I am definitely failing.” And the funniest part is that none of those conversations can change a single answer you have already written.

So, if you can, don't analyse the paper immediately. Let it go. Go home, eat something you like, take a shower, sleep, meet someone you love, watch a movie, go for a walk or simply sit somewhere quietly. Do something that reminds your brain that you are a human being and not a machine built exclusively to answer questions under a three-hour timer.

If you have another paper tomorrow, forget this one completely. Not emotionally, but practically. You cannot change Question 5 anymore. You can still answer tomorrow's Question 5. Your attention belongs to the paper that is still in front of you.

This is where the idea of control becomes useful. Before the examination, your preparation was within your control. During the examination, your answers were within your control. Once you submit the paper, the result is no longer fully within your control. So don't waste the next few hours trying to control something that has already left your hands.

You will remember the question you got wrong. You will suddenly remember the answer you should have written while brushing your teeth. Your brain may replay the paper at 2 a.m. and tell you, “If only I had written that one line.” Let it happen and let it pass. You are not going to rewrite the answer in your head, and you certainly don't need to punish yourself for something that cannot be changed.

If you have multiple papers, don't carry yesterday's paper into tomorrow's. One bad paper does not automatically destroy the attempt, and one excellent paper does not guarantee it either. Your attempt is still being built paper by paper. Give the next paper the attention it deserves.

Thank the People Who Helped You After the final paper, there is one thing I genuinely want you to do: thank the people who helped you.

Call your teacher. Send them a message. Tell them you are grateful. Not because they guaranteed your result, but because they were part of your journey. Somewhere along the way, their explanation made a difficult topic easier. Maybe they repeated something ten times because students kept asking. Maybe they uploaded a revision lecture late at night. Maybe they prepared the notes you kept revising until the last day.

I personally believe we should acknowledge these people. We often remember the marks and forget the people who helped us get there.

You can even go back and watch a small part of a lecture you studied months ago, not to study, but simply to remember where you started. There is something beautiful about hearing the same teacher explain a concept that once looked impossible and realising, “I actually know this now.”

Let Yourself Be Happy Once the final paper is over, allow yourself to be happy. Don't make your happiness conditional on the result.

You may have spent months telling yourself, “I'll celebrate when I clear,” “I'll relax when the result comes,” or “I'll be happy when I become a CS.” Don't do that. You don't know what tomorrow's result will bring, but you know what today brought. Today, you finished something difficult. You showed up, sat through those papers and gave the attempt everything you reasonably could.

That deserves to be acknowledged.

Go out. Eat something good. Meet your friends. Sleep without setting an alarm for a lecture. Watch the movie you kept postponing. Spend time with your family. Do whatever makes you feel like yourself again. You don't have to immediately turn the end of one challenge into the beginning of another.

And if the result doesn't go the way you wanted, remember that an examination result is information, not a verdict on your worth. It tells you something about your preparation and performance in that particular attempt. It does not tell you whether you are intelligent, whether you will succeed in your career or whether you are capable of becoming the professional you want to become.

Take the result seriously, but don't take it personally. Analyse what happened, understand what needs to change and decide what you will do next. A failed attempt can give you useful information if you are willing to look at it honestly. It does not have to become an identity.

And if you pass, then please, for God's sake, celebrate properly.

Call your parents. Call your teachers. Call the friend who listened to you complain for months. Take the picture. Eat something good. Cry if you want to. Laugh loudly. Enjoy the moment.

For at least one day, don't think about the next qualification, the next certificate, the next job or the next target. You don't have to immediately convert your success into another task.\You are allowed to enjoy your own victory.

Look Back Before You Look Ahead There is something beautiful hidden inside almost every long journey: you spend so much time looking at the destination that you forget to notice the person you became while travelling towards it.

When you started CS, you didn't know exactly what was waiting for you. You struggled with subjects, changed teachers, changed your study methods, made mistakes, lost motivation, found it again and somehow continued. You learned how to sit with boredom, work without motivation, deal with failure and keep going even when the result was uncertain.

You may not notice that transformation because it happened slowly. But it happened.

The student who started the journey and the person walking out of that examination centre are not exactly the same. You know more. You have experienced more. You have tested yourself in ways that you probably didn't understand when you started.

So when the examination is finally over, don't immediately ask, “What's next?” For once, look back. Look at the person who started and then look at the person sitting here now.

Maybe you didn't do everything perfectly. Maybe you made mistakes. Maybe there were days when you wasted time, days when you didn't study enough and days when you wanted to quit. It doesn't matter. You still made it this far.

And sometimes that is worth acknowledging.

“Bhai, we made it this far.”

Whatever the result says later, that part is already true.

Now Go Live a Little After months of studying, your brain may not know what to do with itself. You may feel strangely empty. You have been living according to the next chapter, the next lecture, the next revision and the next examination for so long that suddenly having nothing to prepare for can feel unusual.

That's okay.

Don't immediately fill that empty space with another target. Give yourself some time. Sleep properly. Spend time with people. Go somewhere. Read something completely unrelated to CS. Do things you postponed during preparation.

The books can wait. There will always be another examination, another job, another promotion, another skill to learn and another goal to chase. If you spend your entire life waiting for the next achievement before allowing yourself to live, you will eventually realise that you were so busy reaching the next destination that you forgot to experience the journey.

12

Skills You Need to Develop Alongside the Course

8 min read

I am not going to give you the same list of skills that you have probably heard a thousand times already.

Communication. Time management. Networking. Leadership. Teamwork.

Yes, yes, I know. They are important. Every career article, every seminar, every senior on LinkedIn has already told you that you need them. I don't disagree. But after spending years studying for the course, going through training, working in the corporate environment and actually seeing how things work, I think there are a few much more practical skills that nobody talks about enough. These are not the glamorous skills. Nobody is going to give you a certificate for most of them. You probably won't even mention them on your resume. But they can make your life considerably easier during your internship—and some of them can even help you get that internship in the first place.

Let me start with something extremely basic:

MS WORD.

Yes, MS Word. And no, I am not joking.

When I say learn MS Word, I don't mean learn how to type your name, make it bold and change the font to Times New Roman. I mean actually learn how to use it properly.

Because once you enter the corporate world as a CS trainee, you are going to realise something very quickly: a surprising amount of your life is going to happen inside a Word document.

BMRs, minutes, agendas, policies, notices, letters, reports, drafts, resolutions and documents that somehow come back to you five times for “small formatting changes.” You will spend a lot of time creating, editing, reviewing and formatting documents.

Think about it this way. When you were in school, you wouldn't go to class without your notebook. Your notebook was where you wrote, organised and maintained everything you learned. In a corporate environment, MS Word becomes something very similar for a CS.

So learn it properly.

Learn how styles work. Learn page breaks and section breaks. Learn headers and footers, page numbering, tables, Track Changes, comments, formatting, Find and Replace, and all those little features that look boring until someone asks you to use them at 6:30 in the evening and you have absolutely no idea how.

You don't have to become an MS Word wizard. But you should be comfortable enough that when someone gives you a twenty-page document and says, “Make this look professional,” your first reaction isn't to open YouTube.

And while you are learning Word, there is another ridiculously basic skill I want you to learn:

TOUCH TYPING.

If you currently type while looking at the keyboard, searching for every letter like you're decoding some ancient language, please stop doing that. Learn touch typing.

Aim for at least 50 words per minute. If you can get higher, even better. I know what you might be thinking: How is typing speed even a skill for a Company Secretary?

Technically, it isn't going to make you a better lawyer or improve your understanding of SEBI regulations. But it will make you faster at almost everything involving a computer. Emails, minutes, drafts, notes, research, documentation—you do these things repeatedly. Saving a few seconds here and there sounds insignificant, until you realise you are doing it thousands of times over the course of your career.

And, honestly, it creates a small impression too. Imagine two trainees sitting next to each other. One is typing with two fingers, looking down at the keyboard after every few words. The other is just sitting there— tic tic tic tic tic tic tic...

Done.

I am literally writing this book because I can comfortably type at an average of 60+ words per minute. I don't have to think about where the letters are anymore. My brain thinks about the sentence, and my fingers just do their job. It sounds stupidly small. It isn't.

You can use a website named www.monkeytype.com to practise your typing speed. And if you really want to learn this skill from scratch, use a web app called www.typingmaster.com, or you can just search for it on YouTube.

Then comes another skill that you will use almost every single day: EMAIL WRITING.

Corporate communication happens through email. A lot of it. And I genuinely don't understand why we spend years preparing students for professional careers without teaching them how to write a professional email.

You should know how to write a proper subject line. You should know how to ask for something without writing a three-paragraph story. You should know when to keep someone in CC, when not to use Reply All, how to attach documents, how to follow up, how to acknowledge an email and how to communicate something clearly without sounding either rude or ridiculously formal.

And please don't confuse professional email writing with complicated English.

You don't need fancy vocabulary.

You need clarity.

The person reading your email should not have to finish it and wonder, “Okay... but what exactly does this person want from me?” A good professional email usually makes three things clear: what happened, what you need and what action is expected. That's it.

Learn this early. It is one of those skills that looks extremely basic until you work with someone who is terrible at it. Then you suddenly realise how valuable clarity actually is.

Another thing I strongly recommend learning alongside your course is HOW RECRUITMENT ACTUALLY WORKS.

Don't wait until you are desperate for an internship to learn how to make a resume. Understand resumes. Understand ATS. Understand how recruiters shortlist candidates. Understand what a job description is actually telling you. Learn how to describe your internship experience properly. Learn how to write a decent professional summary. Learn how interviews work.

Because there is a difference between being capable and getting the opportunity to prove that you are capable.

Your knowledge doesn't get you into the interview room by itself. Your resume might.

And your resume doesn't get you the job by itself either. Your interview might.

And once you get the opportunity, then your actual skills, attitude and ability to learn start doing the work.

So don't treat resume building as something you will figure out at the end of your CS journey. Start understanding it much earlier. Your first resume will probably be terrible. That's fine. Make it, get feedback, improve it, use it, improve it again.

Which brings me to one of the most underrated skills of all: Stop Being Afraid of Talking to People Seriously, stop being afraid of talking to people. Call someone. Talk to someone you don't know. Introduce yourself. Ask a question. I know this sounds easy when someone else says it, but when you are actually standing there with your phone in your hand, your brain suddenly starts producing a documentary about every possible way the conversation could go wrong. What if they don't respond? What if they think I'm stupid? What if I don't know what to say next? What if they do? So what? You will survive.

One of the easiest ways to become better at talking to people is to stop trying so hard to be interesting and instead become interested. If you don't know what to say, ask an open-ended question. Ask someone how they got into their field, what kind of work they do, what they have learned, or what they would recommend to someone starting out. Appreciate something they have done and, most importantly, actually listen to their answer. You don't need some magical networking script. You need basic human interaction: ask, listen, appreciate and follow up.

There are endless books, courses and techniques on communication, networking and breaking the ice. Read them if you want. But don't become the person who has read twelve books about communication and still cannot call someone because they are "not comfortable with networking." At some point, you have to actually do it. Your first few conversations may be awkward. You might say something stupid, forget someone's name or run out of things to say. That's fine. You are learning. The goal is not to become perfect at conversations; it is to become comfortable enough to start them.

This ability will help you far beyond your training. You will need it when speaking to a senior, coordinating with another department, dealing with a client, approaching a professional, attending a conference, asking someone for guidance or simply walking into a room where you don't know anyone. The ability to communicate with people comfortably can open doors that technical knowledge alone cannot.

And this is exactly what I mean when I talk about developing skills alongside your CS preparation. The technical side of the profession will come through your studies and training. You will learn the Companies Act, SEBI regulations, filings, minutes, Board processes, compliances and everything else that comes with being a Company Secretary. But nobody is necessarily going to sit beside you and teach you how to type properly, write a professional email, improve your resume or become comfortable speaking to someone new. You have to build those skills yourself.

The good news is that you don't need to master everything before starting your training. Start alongside the course. Spend a little time every week improving one practical skill. Learn an MS Word feature. Practise typing for fifteen minutes. Write better emails. Improve your resume. Have one conversation with someone new. These things may look insignificant today, but they compound over time.

When you finally enter your training, you don't want to be the person who knows the theory but needs help with every basic task. You want to be the trainee who can listen carefully, understand what is being asked, open the document, make the changes, draft the email, send it, pick up the phone when required and then ask intelligent questions when the actual technical problem begins. That is the kind of person people enjoy working with, and it gives you a much stronger starting point for your CS career.

So don't wait until you become confident to start talking to people. Talk to people, make a few awkward conversations, learn from them and become confident through experience. You don't need to become a great networker. You simply need to become comfortable being a human being around other human beings.

13

Uncommon Answers to Common Questions: No BullShit

14 min read

There are some questions almost every CS trainee asks at some point. Should I finish my exams first? Should I start training now? Firm or company? Should I stay at the same place for all 21 months? Do attempts matter? What skills should I learn? Should I do another degree?

You will find plenty of answers to these questions. Some will come from seniors, some from teachers, some from LinkedIn, and some from that one person in your batch who somehow has an opinion about everything. But not every answer is useful. The answer that sounds good in theory doesn't always work when you are actually sitting in an office, trying to understand a Board agenda, checking an MCA form, reading an annual report, preparing a disclosure or figuring out why your senior has returned the same draft for the fourth time.

So here are 20 questions I think every CS trainee should ask—not because there is one perfect answer to each of them, but because asking the right question can save you a lot of unnecessary time.

1. Should I complete all my CS exams first or start training alongside?

A lot of students think they should first clear every CS examination and then start training. I don't necessarily agree with that. If you can manage both, I would actually prefer doing them together. There is something very useful about studying a provision in the morning and then seeing that provision being applied in the real world. Suddenly, it isn't just something you have to remember for six marks. You understand why the compliance exists, where the information comes from, what documents are required, who is responsible and what happens when something goes wrong.

There is also a practical advantage—you save time and money. Why unnecessarily stretch the journey if you can build your qualification and experience together? And perhaps the biggest benefit is confidence. When you eventually qualify, you don't want to be someone who has cleared every examination but is afraid of handling actual work. You want to have some understanding of how the professional world operates. Don't just complete the qualification. Build the professional version of yourself alongside it.

2. Should I spend all 21 months at the same organisation?

You can, but you don't necessarily have to. If you find a place where you have a good mentor, meaningful work, decent exposure and an environment where you are genuinely learning, there is absolutely nothing wrong with

completing your entire training there.

But I don't understand the idea that staying at one place for 21 months is automatically better. Training is about exposure, and sometimes one organisation can give you tremendous exposure while sometimes it cannot.

A PCS firm may expose you to multiple clients and different kinds of assignments. A listed company may expose you to Board processes, stock exchange compliances, corporate governance and a completely different scale of work. Experiencing both can make you a more adaptable professional. Of course, don't change places just because another organisation has a bigger name. Change for a reason. Your 21 months should build your career, not just complete your training requirement.

3. What if I realise that my first training choice was a mistake?

Then accept that you made a mistake. This sounds simple, but many trainees struggle with it. They realise within a few months that they aren't learning, the work isn't what they expected or the environment isn't suitable for them. Yet they continue because they think, “I've already spent six months here. Now I have to complete it.” Why? Six months of the wrong decision should not become 21 months of the wrong decision.

Give the organisation a fair chance. Don't expect everything to be perfect. Every workplace has boring work, difficult people and days when you question your decision. But if you have genuinely tried and there is no meaningful learning or growth, consider changing through the proper NOC and training process. Don't stay somewhere wrong just because you are afraid that changing will look bad. A wrong first decision is a mistake. Staying there despite knowing it is wrong is a choice.

4. Firm or company—which one should I choose?

This question becomes much easier when you stop asking, “Which one is better?” and start asking, “Better for what?” If you want to build a career in practice, a good PCS firm can be incredibly valuable. You get exposure to different clients, industries and problems and learn how professional services actually work. If you want to build a corporate career, especially in governance, securities law or listed-company compliance, corporate exposure becomes important.

Personally, if your end goal is corporate, I see a lot of value in starting with a good firm for around 6–7 months and then moving into a listed company. The firm can give you breadth, while the listed company can give you depth and exposure to structured corporate processes. But this isn't a formula. A trainee doing meaningful work in a small firm can learn more than someone sitting in a famous organisation doing repetitive administrative work. Don't choose the organisation first. Choose the professional you want to become.

5. Should I pursue a Bachelor's degree along with CS?

Yes. Absolutely. I don't see why you would unnecessarily close an academic door while pursuing a professional qualification. CS is a professional qualification. A Bachelor's degree gives you an academic foundation and keeps other opportunities open. You may eventually decide to do an MBA, law, finance, a specialised qualification or something completely different.

And no, I don't believe that doing graduation means you aren't serious about CS. You don't have to choose between becoming a Company Secretary and becoming an educated professional. If you can manage your time responsibly, pursue both. The bigger point is this: you are making career decisions at an age when you probably don't know exactly where you will be ten years from now. So why unnecessarily reduce your options? Your degree doesn't compete with your CS qualification. It complements it.

6. Do attempts matter?

The number of attempts by itself doesn't tell me much about a person. Someone can clear CS in the first attempt and still struggle professionally. Someone else can take several attempts and eventually become an excellent professional. What matters is what happened between those attempts. Did you identify your mistakes? Did your preparation change? Did your writing improve? Did you change your revision strategy? Did you understand why you failed?

One failed attempt can teach you discipline. Another can teach you resilience. But if you keep failing for the same reason and keep using the same strategy, then yes, the attempts start telling a different story. The problem isn't failing; the problem is failing without learning. An attempt is a number. What you learn from it is your story.

7. Should I focus only on CS subjects during training?

No. Your CS syllabus is the foundation of your professional knowledge, not the boundary of it. Learn Excel. Learn how to read financial statements. Understand annual reports. Read SEBI regulations. Learn drafting. Understand Board processes. Learn how businesses actually make money. Learn how to research something you don't know.

And please don't become the person who says, “This isn't in my syllabus.” The company doesn't care whether the problem was in your syllabus. The client doesn't care. The Board doesn't care. The regulator certainly doesn't care. You are entering a profession, not preparing for one more examination. Your syllabus tells you what to study. Curiosity tells you what to learn.

8. What should I actually learn during my training?

Don't measure your training by the number of forms you filed. Instead, measure it by the number of things you can eventually handle without someone holding your hand. Can you understand why a Board approval is required? Can you prepare a first draft of a resolution? Can you research a legal provision? Can you understand a stock exchange disclosure? Can you follow a compliance from start to finish? Can you read an annual report and understand what the company is doing?

These are the things that gradually separate someone who has completed training from someone who has actually used training. Your first few months might be about following instructions. Eventually, the goal should be to understand the instructions, and after that, to start anticipating what needs to happen next. The real progress is from “Tell me what to do” to “I think this needs to be done—let me verify it.”

9. Should I try to learn everything during training?

No. And this is something young professionals need to hear more often. There is a strange pressure to know everything. Everyone is learning securities law, insolvency, ESG, AI, finance, Excel, communication, public speaking and probably trying to become a content creator at the same time. Relax. You don't need to master everything at twenty-two.

Start by becoming genuinely good at a few things. Understand them properly. Learn the logic behind them. Then expand. Someone who understands five areas deeply is often more useful than someone who has read the names of fifty regulations but cannot apply any of them. Eventually, you need breadth and depth, but you don't need both immediately. Breadth makes you aware. Depth makes you valuable.

10. Should I ask questions or try to figure everything out myself?

Ask questions, but don't ask lazy questions. There is a massive difference between saying, “Sir, what do I do?” and saying, “I checked the provision and I think this requirement applies, but I'm confused about whether this exemption is applicable in our case. Am I understanding it correctly?” The second person is still asking a question, but they have already done some work.

Nobody expects a trainee to know everything. In fact, if you never ask questions during training, I would be more concerned than if you ask too many. Just make sure you are not outsourcing your thinking to your senior. Don't be afraid of asking questions. Be afraid of becoming dependent on questions.

11. What if my senior gives me boring or repetitive work?

Do it. Not every day of your training is going to involve attending Board meetings or drafting important legal opinions. Sometimes you'll check data for three hours. Sometimes you'll update a register. Sometimes you'll correct formatting. Sometimes you'll prepare the same document again because somebody changed two words. That's work.

But don't let repetitive work become repetitive learning. If you're doing something again and again, start understanding the process behind it. Why are you doing it? Where does the data come from? What happens after you finish it? Who checks it? What can go wrong? And once you understand the process, ask yourself whether there is a way to make it faster or more accurate. Never waste a boring task. There is usually a system hiding behind it.

12. Should I choose training based on the stipend?

Money matters. Let's not pretend it doesn't. You have expenses, travel costs, family responsibilities and your own financial goals, so there is nothing wrong with considering the stipend. But don't make it your only filter. You are spending 21 months of your life there. You should also ask what you are receiving in return—exposure, mentorship, practical knowledge, responsibility and professional confidence.

At the same time, don't romanticise being underpaid by calling everything “learning.” Your work has value. The ideal situation is simple: find a place where you are learning and where the compensation is fair for your circumstances. Don't sell 21 months of your career for a slightly better stipend. But don't sell your work for “exposure” either.

13. Should I compare my progress with other trainees?

You will. You probably can't completely avoid it. Someone will clear before you. Someone will get a better training opportunity. Someone will join a listed company. Someone will get a higher stipend. Someone will have 10,000 LinkedIn followers while you're still trying to write your first post. Let them.

The problem isn't seeing someone else's progress. The problem is using it as evidence that you are failing. Your career isn't a race where everyone has to reach the finish line at the same time. Instead, compare yourself with the person you were six months ago. Are you more confident? Can you handle more responsibility? Do you understand more? Can you solve problems faster? Don't compare your chapter two with someone else's chapter ten.

14. Is LinkedIn important for a CS trainee?

Yes, but not as much as becoming good at your actual work. LinkedIn can help you build visibility, meet professionals, discover opportunities and document your learning. You can share something you learned from a Board meeting, a compliance, an annual report or even a mistake you made. But don't confuse posting about compliance with understanding compliance. You can have thousands of followers and still be unable to handle a basic professional task.

Use LinkedIn to document your journey, not manufacture one. Your online profile should eventually become a reflection of your professional development—not a substitute for it. Visibility can open the door. Competence decides whether you stay in the room.

15. Should I specialise early?

Have an area you are curious about, but don't turn it into a cage. Maybe you love securities law. Maybe corporate governance interests you. Maybe you enjoy insolvency. Maybe ESG excites you. Maybe you discover that you actually enjoy drafting more than you expected. Explore it.

But don't feel pressured to decide your entire professional life during training. Your interests will change when you experience real work. Something that sounds boring in a textbook may become fascinating when you see its practical impact. Something you thought you loved may become exhausting when you do it every day. Your first goal isn't to find your forever niche. Your first goal is to become professionally useful. Explore early. Specialise when you understand yourself better.

16. Should a CS learn technology and AI?

You don't need to become a software engineer, but you absolutely should become comfortable with technology. The profession is changing. A lot of repetitive work can be automated. Information can be found faster. Documents can be analysed faster. Data can be organised faster. AI can assist with research, drafting, summarisation and productivity.

But there is an important catch: AI doesn't remove your responsibility to verify. If an AI tool gives you a section number, regulation, case law or interpretation, you still need to check it. If you put confidential company information into a tool without understanding the organisation's policies, you can create a completely different problem. So learn AI, automation, Excel and the tools your organisation uses. The future professional won't necessarily be the person who knows the most about technology. It will be the person who knows where technology can improve professional judgement without replacing it. Don't compete with technology at doing repetitive work. Learn how to use technology to do better work.

17. Should I accept every opportunity during training?

No. This may sound strange when everyone keeps telling you to “grab every opportunity,” but your time is limited. Not every webinar deserves your Saturday. Not every certificate adds value. Not every competition improves your career. Not every networking event is networking.

Before saying yes, ask yourself what you are actually getting from it. Will you learn something? Build a useful skill? Meet someone relevant? Create meaningful work? Improve your credibility? If yes, go for it. If you're doing it only because everyone else is doing it, think again. Being busy can feel productive because your calendar looks full, but your career doesn't grow because your calendar is full. Learn to say no to things that make you busy but don't make you better.

18. When should I start thinking about my career after qualification?

Before qualification. Much before. Don't wait until your final result is declared and then suddenly start asking, “What job should I apply for?” Training gives you 21 months to observe yourself. Do you enjoy practice? Do you prefer corporate work? Do you enjoy securities law? Do you like governance? Do you enjoy drafting? Do you like client interaction? Do you want to work in a listed company? Do you want to eventually build your own practice?

You don't need all the answers immediately, but you should start collecting evidence. Every assignment, department, senior and difficult task is giving you information about what kind of professional you might want to become. Don't wait until training ends to start building the career training was supposed to prepare you for.

19. What if I don't feel confident during training?

Good. Seriously. You are a trainee. You aren't supposed to walk into your first week knowing everything about the Companies Act, SEBI regulations, Board procedures and corporate governance. Confidence doesn't magically appear because someone tells you to “believe in yourself.” Real professional confidence comes from evidence.

The first time you prepare something, you may check it ten times. The tenth time, you might check it twice. Eventually, you know what mistakes to look for before anyone tells you. That is confidence. Not pretending, not speaking loudly and not using complicated words, but knowing that even when you don't know something, you know how to find the answer. Confidence is not knowing everything. Confidence is trusting yourself to figure things out.

20. If my training ended tomorrow, would I actually be ready?

This is perhaps the most important question in the entire chapter. Don't ask yourself only, “Have I completed my 21 months?” Ask, “What can I do today that I couldn't do before training?” Can you independently research a provision? Can you identify an applicable compliance? Can you prepare a first draft? Can you understand why a Board approval is required? Can you read an annual report? Can you understand a stock exchange disclosure? Can you follow a compliance from beginning to end? And perhaps the most important one: Do you know what you don't know?

If the answer to some of these questions is no, don't panic. You are still learning. But now you have a direction. Your training was never supposed to be about surviving 21 months, collecting a certificate and moving on. It was supposed to turn you from a student who knows the law into a professional who can apply it.

And when those 21 months are finally over, the best feeling shouldn't be, “Thank God, my training is completed.” It should be, “Okay. Now give me the problem. I'll figure it out.”

The goal was never to complete 21 months. The goal was to become someone worth those 21 months.

14

Bonus Chapter for Trainees

6 min read

These are some of the things I wish someone had told me before I started my 21 months of training. None of them are complicated, and you may already have heard some of them before. But simple advice becomes powerful when you actually follow it. Training is not only about completing your required months; it is your first real exposure to how professionals work, communicate, think and build relationships. So while you learn the technical side of the profession, pay attention to the game around it.

1. Never outshine your master. This is the first law in Robert Greene's The 48 Laws of Power, and there is some truth hidden inside it. Your trainer is not your competitor. You may sometimes know something they don't, find an error they missed, or have a better way of doing something. Don't turn that into a demonstration of your superiority. Make your trainer's work easier, give credit generously and correct things without making people feel small. The objective is not to prove that you are smarter; it is to become the person your senior trusts with important work.

2. For the first few months, keep your mouth shut and observe. You don't know the organisation yet. You don't know who actually makes decisions, how people communicate, what your senior expects, which problems are important and which ones are not. Watch everything. Listen to how emails are written, how meetings are conducted, how seniors speak to clients and how mistakes are handled. You will learn things nobody will teach you. And remember, you don't have to give an opinion every time you have one. Sometimes saying less than necessary is a professional skill.

3. Understand your trainer and make their work easier. Learn how they like things done. If they hate incomplete drafts, don't send incomplete drafts. If they want an update before a deadline, give it before they ask. Check your work before putting your name on it. Try to reach a point where your trainer thinks, "Give it to him; he'll handle it." That is how trust is built. Naval often speaks about becoming exceptionally good at something that is naturally yours; during training, your first leverage is simply becoming exceptionally reliable. Your aim should be to make yourself valuable, not merely busy.

4. Learn corporate language and communication. Being technically correct is only half the job. Learn how professionals communicate. Read your seniors' emails. Notice how they disagree without sounding aggressive, how they ask for approvals, how they escalate an issue and how they communicate a problem to management. Learn the difference between casual English and corporate English. A Company Secretary may know the law, but a good Company Secretary also knows how to communicate the law to a director who has no interest in reading the law.

5. Record your work. I used to mail important work to myself and maintain my own record of what I had worked on and learned. Do something similar. Keep a private record of projects, compliances, concepts, mistakes, formats and problems you solved. Do not take confidential company information with you, but record what you learned from the experience. After 21 months, this becomes your personal library and later, your portfolio of experience. Ankur Warikoo's idea of documenting the journey is useful here: don't wait until you have an impressive career to create evidence of your work. Start recording the journey while it is happening.

6. Save money during training. Your stipend may not feel like much, but don't spend every rupee simply because you received it. Keep something aside every month for your own professional development. There will be CLDPs, conferences, workshops, courses, books, travel and opportunities that may cost ₹35,000–₹40,000 or more. When a genuinely valuable opportunity arrives, you don't want money to be the reason you cannot take it. Learn to think in terms of investment rather than expenditure. Some things you buy will make you poorer; some things you buy will make you more capable.

7. Build your reputation before you need it. You don't need to become an influencer. You need to become findable. Write about what you are learning, record useful work where it is appropriate, explain a difficult concept, share a project or document your journey. Naval's idea of leverage applies here: something you create once can continue working for you long after you have created it. Your LinkedIn profile, articles, projects and body of work can become evidence of what you can do. Don't manufacture expertise. Document genuine learning.

8. Learn beyond the syllabus. Your training is a rare period where you can observe law, business, finance, people and technology at the same time. Don't reduce yourself to someone who knows how to file forms. Understand why the company is doing something, where the money comes from, how decisions are made, what management actually cares about and where technology can remove unnecessary work. Ask better questions. Read annual reports. Study businesses. Learn Excel, Word, communication, AI and basic finance. Your qualification may tell people what you studied; your additional skills will tell them what you can actually do.

9. Don't try to look successful; become useful. This is one of the simplest principles you can carry through your career. Don't chase designations, followers or impressive words before you have something valuable behind them. Become the person who solves problems. Become the person who can be trusted. Become the person who finishes what they start. The reputation will follow. Your first 21 months are not the time to prove that you have arrived. They are the time to quietly build the person who will eventually arrive.

And finally, remember that training is temporary, but the habits you develop during it are not. You are learning much more than compliance. You are learning how to deal with people, how to communicate, how to observe power, how to handle responsibility, how to create value and how to think for yourself. Take the work seriously, but don't take the hierarchy too seriously. Learn from everyone, become useful to everyone, and keep building something that belongs to you.

10. Invest in learning before you invest for the sake of investing. If you are genuinely interested in investing and understand what you are doing, absolutely start early. But don't force yourself to put ₹500 into an SIP every month just so you can say you are an investor, while simultaneously telling yourself that a ₹500 book or a ₹2,000 course is too expensive. During your training years, your highest-returning asset is still yourself. If there is a course you genuinely want to take, take it. If there is a book you want to read, buy it. Books are one of the closest things we have to a cheat code; you can spend a few hundred rupees and access years of someone's thinking, mistakes and experience. That can have a far higher return on your life than a small investment made without understanding what you are doing. The same applies to IPOs: don't confuse the excitement of making a quick return with investing. If you don't understand what you are buying, keep your money. Invest in your ability to earn before obsessing over tiny returns on money you haven't learned to manage yet.

11. Create a digital presence. You don't need to become an influencer, and you certainly don't need to turn your life into content. Just be present. In today's professional world, being good is valuable, but being discoverable is an advantage. For a CS trainee, LinkedIn is probably the simplest place to start. Put your real work, learning and interests there. Write occasionally about something you genuinely learned, share a useful observation, document a project or simply let people know what you are working towards. Don't manufacture a personality because you think the algorithm likes it. Build a digital record of who you are becoming. Naval's idea of leverage applies here: your work should not always depend on your physical presence. Something useful that you write today can still be found by a recruiter, founder or professional years later. You don't need thousands of followers. You just need to exist when someone searches your name

A Final Note

1 min read

If you made it this far, thank you for reading.

Burn the Sea is not about doing something impossible just for the sake of being different. It is about questioning the boundaries you have accepted, especially when everyone around you tells you that there is only one way forward. Sometimes there is no bridge, no clear path and no guarantee that your idea will work. But that does not always mean you should turn back. Sometimes you have to create your own way.

For me, writing this book was one such attempt. I did not know whether anyone would read it, whether it would become successful or whether I was experienced enough to write it. I simply didn't want to spend years wondering what would have happened if I had tried. So I tried.

That is what Burn the Sea means to me: don't let the absence of a path become the reason you never begin.

If this book made you think differently about your CS journey, your career or yourself, I would genuinely like to hear from you. You can write to me at wewillburnthesea@gmail.com or connect with me on LinkedIn.

And if this book helped you, please consider sharing your honest thoughts on LinkedIn and mentioning me. Your words might reach another CS student who needs to hear them.

Thank you for reading.
-Jatin Nodiya
